(Fitterfly, 23 Apr 2025) [D3-04-F43] | "Now my HBA1c reduced to 6.1 and medicine also reduced to half." (Fitterfly, 10 Nov 2024) [D3-04-F44] |
61	
62	None of the 300 reviews mentions language or voice, and none describes a dose change from a home reading (count from the research note's method section).
63	
64	### Reminders and messages
65	
66	In a Punjab trial at two public hospitals, 388 patients with uncontrolled pressure got two myth-busting WhatsApp reminders before their visit or none; attendance was 21.8% against 19.6%, a null result, and beliefs did not change [D3-04-F50]. A Delhi study of 110 patients (counselling, voice calls, SMS) reported control rising from 14.7% to 52.9%, with no control group [D3-04-F51].
67	The phone is often not the patient's. Caregivers enable access and devices are shared [D3-04-F05]; one review moves a meter from a husband's phone to a mother's [D3-04-F25]. 54% of women aged 15-49 own the phone they use, 46.6% in rural areas [D3-04-F23]. Among 150 rural older adults near Mysore, 50% owned a phone, few a smartphone, and digital literacy was 11% [D3-04-F56]. About 10.6% of Indians spoke English in 2011 [D3-04-F57].
68	
69	So what for us (OUR VIEW): a message only works if it reaches the person who holds the phone and leads to a decision.
70	
71	### Two field voices from people who run programmes
72	
73	Both are LinkedIn posts, paraphrased; numbers inside them are unverified.
74	
75	- A national NCD (non-communicable disease) consultant at UNICEF India, about Apr 2026: programmes failed on BP machines uncalibrated for months and mid-month drug stock-outs; one protocol, steady supply and the Simple app made missed visits visible. Claims control rose 48 percentage points in primary care and 23 in secondary (POST CLAIM, source not named) (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026).
76	- A doctor and WHO consultant, about Oct 2026: counting visits is not enough; programmes must know who continues, who is controlled and who missed follow-up. Cites mWellcare: a digital system does not guarantee results (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026).
77	
78	Neither describes dose changes from home readings.
79	
80	### What we could not find
81	
82	A household figure for cuff ownership; any Indian clinician voice on dose steps from home readings; any patient voice on a dose increase; voice against text preference among older patients; Reddit posts (the archive timed out) and Google Play reviews.
83	
84	### So what for us
85	
86	OUR VIEW:
87	- **Assume most patients do not own a cuff.** Supply one and teach the technique; only 18.1% used one even among clinic attenders [D3-04-F06].
88	- **A doctor may not trust the state protocol.** Each proposal must show why the step is safe, answering the fears of slow control and side effects [D3-04-F15].
89	- **Never rely on a reminder alone.** WhatsApp reminders did not raise attendance [D3-04-F50]; the reading must lead to a decision.
90	- **Design for the household phone.** Reach whoever holds it, by voice, in the local language [D3-04-F05, D3-04-F23].
91	- **Risk: home readings bring bad news.** 21.8% of treated clinic attenders had masked uncontrolled pressure [D3-04-F09]; expect fear of more drugs and the urge to stop [D3-04-F02].

3	### What this part shows
4	
5	Across six disease areas, a home reading improved outcomes when it led to a changed treatment, and mostly did not when it was only displayed or turned into a reminder. This part sets out the trials behind that pattern, their safety record, the Indian results (including one important null result), and what a doctor would need before trusting a product built on them.
6

12	
13	Each row sets a result where the reading changed the treatment beside one where it was only shown or used for a reminder. OUR VIEW: the sorting is ours; the numbers are from the notes.

16	|---|---|---|

Patient self-titration: -9.2 mmHg at 12 months [D1-01-F02]. Pharmacists adjusting drugs: 57.2% against 30.0% controlled [D1-01-F04]. | Self-monitoring alone: -1.0 mmHg (95% CI -3.3 to 1.2), no effect [D1-01-F05]. Reminder app: -0.5 mmHg, p=0.78 [D1-01-F06]. |
18	| Heart failure | Full guideline doses within 2 weeks of discharge: readmission or death 15.2% against 23.3% (adjusted 180-day estimates; the arm also had 4 clinic visits and more side effects, 41% against 29%), RR 0.66 [D1-01-F27]. Structured remote management: all-cause death HR 0.70 [D1-01-F30]. | Daily symptoms and weight sent to own clinicians: 52.3% against 51.5% readmission or death [D1-01-F32]. Telemonitoring reviewed by central nurses with protocol actions and calls, but no mandated dose protocol: aHR 1.03 [D1-01-F33]. Pooled passive telemonitoring: death RR 0.93, not significant [D1-01-F54]. |

20	| Type 2 diabetes | Handheld device computing the next insulin dose: HbA1c (a blood test showing average sugar over about three months) -1.0 against -0.3 [D1-01-F13]. Closed-loop insulin against a glucose sensor alone: HbA1c 0.6 lower, time in range 14 points higher [D1-01-F43]. | Monitoring and coaching tools without a continuous glucose monitor, type 2, US (PHTI): "do not deliver clinically meaningful benefits" [D1-01-F40]. Exception to note: a glucose sensor alone gave HbA1c -0.4 in basal-insulin users [D1-01-F42]. |
21	| Asthma | Patient raises the steroid dose with each reliever puff (SMART): exacerbations RR 0.68 [D1-02-F37]. | Inhaler reminders: adherence 84% against 30%, school absence 1.9% against 1.7% of days, no difference [D1-02-F01]. Sensor inhaler system: odds ratio for control 1.35, credible interval 0.846 to 2.038, crossing 1 [D1-02-F02]. |
22	| Tuberculosis adherence | No trial in the notes changed the treatment from adherence data. In China the planned step (doctor moves non-adherent patients to intensive management) was "underutilised" [D1-02-F34]. | Smart pillboxes or labels, four countries, 23,483 patients: poor outcomes not reduced (adjusted ratios 1.13 to 1.49, all intervals crossing 1) [D1-02-F59]. |
23	
24	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the active ingredient is the treatment change, not the sensor and not the nudge. A product that stops at showing a reading sits in the right-hand column, where results are mostly null.

27	
28	![Share of patients under control with and without a programme that steps the dose](adaptive-care-pictures/21-share-controlled.png)

32	Blood pressure has the deepest evidence: primary-care titration trials, a 33,995-person trial of dose stepping by village health workers with four-year hard outcomes, and South Asian and Indian trials, including a null result that shows where a product should not try to add value.

34	#### (a) Trials where home readings led to a medicine change

A pooled analysis of individual patient data from 15 trials (7,138 people) found self-monitoring worked best in people on fewer drugs and with baseline systolic up to 170 [D1-01-F05].
44	
45	#### (b) Dose stepping by non-physicians at scale
46	
47	The China Rural Hypertension Control Project (CRHCP) was an open cluster trial in 326 villages with 33,995 people aged 40 and over [D1-01-F09]. Village doctors (community health workers) started and stepped drugs by a standard protocol, supervised by primary-care physicians, and coached patients on home BP monitoring. The comparator was enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09].
48	
49	- **18 months:** BP under 130/80 in 57.0% against 19.9%, a difference of 37.0 points (95% CI 34.9 to 39.1); systolic 14.5 mmHg lower, diastolic 7.1 lower; no treatment-related serious adverse events [D1-01-F09].
50	- **4 years (median), age 60 and over (22,386 people):** cardiovascular events (heart attack, stroke, heart-failure admission, cardiovascular death) 2.7% against 3.5% a year, HR 0.75 (0.69 to 0.81); all-cause death HR 0.90 (0.83 to 0.98) [D1-01-F38].
51	- **4 years, under 60 (11,609 people):** cardiovascular events HR 0.64 (0.56 to 0.75); stroke 0.64; heart failure 0.39; cardiovascular death 0.54 [D1-01-F38].
52	- **Safety at 4 years:** injurious falls, symptomatic low BP, fainting and kidney outcomes did not differ between groups in either age band [D1-01-F38].
53	
54	The caveat. The trial registry entry (opened by the claims check) says the intervention also gave free or discounted drugs and paid village doctors incentives tied to control rates [D1-01-F38]. The effect therefore cannot be credited to the protocol alone.
55	
56	#### (c) The Indian evidence
57	
58	**The national programme's surveys.** The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) surveyed the same 9 districts in 5 states twice. In 2018-19, of 7,047 people with hypertension, 52.4% were aware, 40.8% treated and 14.5% controlled; in two districts control was under 5% [D1-01-F10]. In 2023-24, of 7,324, 58.5% were aware, 44.7% treated and 21.2% controlled, a gain of 6.7 points in control [D1-01-F11]. This is a before-after survey with no control districts [D1-01-F11]. In the IHCI cohort of 21,895 registered patients, 51% returned for follow-up; among those who returned, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10].
59	
60	**The South Asian trial.** COBRA-BPS was a cluster trial in 30 rural communities in Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka with 2,645 adults with hypertension, run for 24 months [D1-01-F37]. Government community health workers made home visits for BP monitoring and counselling; physicians were trained; care was coordinated in the public sector. Systolic fell 9.0 against 3.9 mmHg, a difference of 5.2 (3.2 to 7.1); control under 140/90 was 53.2% against 43.7%, RR 1.22; all-cause death 2.9% against 4.3%, with no confidence interval in the abstract [D1-01-F37]. Health workers monitored and referred; trained physicians changed the drugs [D1-01-F37]. Post-hoc, patients got about 0.11 more drugs each [D1-01-F12].
61	
62	**The decision-support trial that found nothing.** mWellcare was an open cluster trial in 40 community health centres in India with 3,698 people with hypertension, diabetes or both, run for 12 months [D1-01-F46]. Nurse-managed care with an Android app giving algorithm-based management prompts, a health record and reminders was compared with enhanced usual care. Systolic difference -0.98 mmHg (95% CI -4.64 to 2.67); HbA1c +0.11 (-0.24 to 0.45). Both arms fell by about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. The authors: "We did not find an incremental benefit of mWellcare over enhanced usual care" [D1-01-F46].
63	
64	OUR VIEW, what the null result means:
65	- Prompting a nurse or doctor during a clinic visit added nothing over a well-run protocol programme that already produced a 13 mmHg fall [D1-01-F46].
66	- The app worked at the visit. It did not act on home readings between visits, and it did not reach patients who never came back.
67	
68	OUR VIEW, what it does not mean:
69	- It does not show that between-visit titration fails in India. The notes found no Indian randomised trial of home readings driving a titration protocol (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
70	- It does not show that protocols fail. The enhanced usual-care arm improved as much as the app arm.
71	
72	Contrast a South Asian diabetes trial, CARRS: non-physician care coordinators plus physician decision-support software doubled the chance of improving HbA1c, BP and LDL cholesterol together, RR 2.1 (1.5 to 2.8) at 12 months [D1-01-F23]. OUR VIEW: the extra ingredient was a person following patients up.
73	
74	A secondary analysis of a company-linked Indian diabetes trial (Twin Health) used home BP to guide drug changes: systolic -7.6 against -3.2 mmHg, in small subgroups [D1-01-F20].
75	
76	#### (d) A lifestyle-only prescription app in Japan
77	
78	HERB-DH1 tested CureApp HT, an app giving personalised lifestyle coaching with no drug change (adaptive depth 3), in 390 untreated adults with hypertension at 12 sites in Japan, open-label, for 12 weeks [D1-01-F07]. Against lifestyle advice alone: 24-hour ambulatory systolic -2.4 mmHg (95% CI -4.5 to -0.3), home -4.3, office -3.6; no major programme-related safety events to 24 weeks [D1-01-F07]. CureApp HT was approved in April 2022 and covered by national health insurance from 1 September 2022, prescribed by doctors (THEIR CLAIM for "first worldwide") [D1-01-F57]. A price of about 8,000 yen, with the patient paying 30%, appears in a search summary only [D1-01-F57]; the company's June 2026 release gives 7,010 yen for the app as an insured material (THEIR CLAIM) [D2-04-F43].
79	
80	OUR VIEW: it moved BP about half as much as the titration trials, in patients not yet on drugs; depth 3 helps a little but does not replace dose changes.
81	
82	#### (e) What telemonitoring adds once someone is titrating
83	
84	Little. In TASMINH4, telemonitoring against paper self-monitoring, with the GP titrating in both arms, gave -1.2 mmHg (95% CI -3.5 to 1.2), not significant [D1-01-F03]. The independent US review by PHTI (Peterson Health Technology Institute, October 2024) rated monitoring-only programmes "not clinically meaningful", and said monitoring "may support adoption for providers who consistently act on monitoring data" [D1-01-F39]. It rated medication-management programmes, where virtual care teams adjust drugs, "clinically meaningful and more rapid", against a threshold of a 5 mmHg systolic fall [D1-01-F39].
85	
86	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the authority to change the dose between visits, and someone acting on it, is what worked. Electronics added little once a clinician was titrating. Our product's value must sit where mWellcare did not look: between visits, from home readings, among the half who do not return.
87	
88	### Diabetes
89	
90	In type 2 diabetes the same split holds: software that changes the insulin dose works, and monitoring or coaching alone gives small gains. Closed-loop insulin, where the device changes the dose itself every few minutes, is the model case of an adaptive therapy.
91	
92	**Insulin-dose software (adaptive depth 4).**
93	- d-Nav, 2019: randomised trial, 181 adults on insulin with HbA1c 7.5-11%, 3 US centres, 6 months. A handheld device measured glucose and computed the next dose, plus clinician support, against clinician support alone (both arms 7 contacts). HbA1c fell 1.0% against 0.3% (p<0.0001); low blood sugar 0.29 against 0.29 events a month. Funded by the US NIH [D1-01-F13].
94	- TeleDiab-2, 2019: randomised, 191 adults starting basal (long-acting) insulin, 4 months. A phone voice system and an app both proposed daily dose changes towards a fasting glucose of about 100 mg/dL. HbA1c -1.44% and -1.48% against -0.92%. No severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F14]. The country (France) comes from the research agent's knowledge, not the abstract [D1-01-F14].
95	- Sanofi My Dose Coach has observational data only: in the US, 2,517 users, 44% reached their fasting target, low blood sugar in 12-16% of users [D1-01-F15]; in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, 494 users, 55.9% reached target in a mean 14.8 days, low blood sugar 1.4% [D1-01-F16]. Neither had a control group. Its status in India is unknown (search summary only) [D1-04-F09].
96	
97	**Glucose sensors with and without an algorithm.**
98	- Sensor alone (CGM, continuous glucose monitor), not on insulin: IMMEDIATE, 116 adults, 16 weeks, time in range up 9.9 points, HbA1c 0.3% lower (95% CI 0 to 0.7) [D1-01-F17].
99	- Sensor alone, on basal insulin: MOBILE, 175 adults, 15 US centres, 8 months: HbA1c 0.4% lower (-0.8 to -0.1). Funded by Dexcom, the sensor maker [D1-01-F42].
100	- Sensor plus algorithm: 2IQP, 2025, 319 adults on insulin, US and Canada, 13 weeks. Automated insulin delivery against own insulin method, with a sensor in both arms. HbA1c 0.6 points lower (-0.8 to -0.4); time in range 14 points higher. Funded by Tandem, the pump maker [D1-01-F43]. Because both arms had a sensor, this isolates what the dose-changing algorithm adds.
101	
102	**Closed loop as the model case.** In type 1 diabetes, Control-IQ (168 people, 6 months) raised time in range by 11 points against a sensor-augmented pump and ran in closed-loop mode 90% of the time [D1-01-F24]. The iLet bionic pancreas (326 people, 13 weeks) started from body weight alone with no carbohydrate counting and lowered HbA1c by 0.5 [D1-01-F25]. In type 2 diabetes, a 26-person crossover trial with no meal doses gave time in range 66.3% against 32.3% [D1-01-F26]. A 2026 review says the American Diabetes Association now supports automated delivery as the preferred method for some type 2 patients; the ADA text itself was not opened [D1-01-F45].
103	
104	**Nutrition and "digital twin" results, with caveats.**
105	- Zeevi 2015, Israel, 800 people: a model predicted each person's post-meal glucose; HbA1c was not the outcome [D1-01-F22]. ZOE METHOD (347 US adults, mostly without diabetes, company-sponsored): triglycerides -0.13 mmol/L [D1-01-F55].
106	- Twin Health, India, 319 people, open-label, 2:1: HbA1c -2.9 against -0.3 at 1 year and "72.7% remission"; the remission definition and drug-withdrawal rules are not in the abstract, and author company links were not checked [D1-01-F19].
107	- Twin Health, Cleveland Clinic, 150 people, single site: HbA1c 6.5% or under on no drug except metformin, 71% against 2.4%. Read through a trade article only [D1-01-F56].
108	- Virta: not randomised (262 against 87, self-selected). At 2 years, use of diabetes drugs other than metformin fell from 55.7% to 26.8% [D1-01-F21].
109	
110	**The independent verdict.** PHTI (March 2024) found US digital tools for type 2 diabetes without a continuous glucose monitor "do not deliver clinically meaningful benefits and result in a higher cost than usual care", with gains "minimal and short-term" [D1-01-F40]. The two exceptions were people with higher HbA1c newly starting insulin, and nutritional ketosis programmes [D1-01-F40]. PHTI's new review of sensor and GLP-1 support reports in 2027 [D1-01-F41].
111	
112	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: insulin titration is the second protocol for the same loop and has trial support, but low blood sugar makes it riskier, and the large nutrition effects come from company-linked or non-randomised studies.
113	
114	### Heart failure
115	
116	Heart failure gives the sharpest contrast in the notes: fast dose stepping cut death or readmission by a third, while several large telemonitoring trials without a mandated dose protocol were null.
117	
118	**Fast dose stepping.** STRONG-HF (2022) was an open-label trial in 87 hospitals in 14 countries with 1,078 patients admitted with acute heart failure [D1-01-F27]. The high-intensity arm raised drugs to full recommended doses within 2 weeks of discharge, with 4 visits in 2 months checking symptoms, lab tests and NT-proBNP (a blood marker of heart strain). At day 90, full doses: RAS blockers 55% against 2%, beta blockers 49% against 4%. Readmission or death at 180 days: 15.2% against 23.3% (adjusted estimates, not raw shares), RR 0.66 (0.50 to 0.86); the high-intensity arm also reported more side effects (see Safety). The trial stopped early for benefit. Funder: Roche Diagnostics, maker of NT-proBNP tests [D1-01-F27]. Benefit by age: HR 0.51 under 65, 0.73 over 65, no significant difference [D1-01-F28]. A Russian chatbot titration trial (66 patients, 6 weeks) saw 2 against 16 decompensations or deaths but lost 7 of 33 remote patients [D1-01-F51].
119	
120	**Telemonitoring: positive and negative trials.**
121	
122	| Trial | Patients, place | What happened to the reading | Result |
123	|---|---|---|---|
124	| TELE-HF, 2010 | 1,653, USA | Daily symptoms and weight by phone, reviewed by patients' own clinicians | Readmission or death 52.3% against 51.5%, null [D1-01-F32] |
125	| BEAT-HF, 2016 | 1,437, California | BP, pulse, weight reviewed by central nurses with protocol actions and phone calls; no mandated dose protocol | Readmission aHR 1.03, null; better quality of life [D1-01-F33] |
126	| GUIDE-HF, 2021 | 1,000, US and Canada | Implanted lung-artery pressure sensor guiding care | HR 0.88 (0.74 to 1.05), neutral overall [D1-01-F34] |
127	| TIM-HF2, 2018 | 1,571, Germany | Structured remote management | Days lost ratio 0.80 (p=0.046); death HR 0.70 (0.50 to 0.96) [D1-01-F30] |
128	
129	OUR VIEW on what separates them: the positive trials had a structured team or explicit dose targets; the null ones sent data to clinicians or nurses without a mandated dose protocol (BEAT-HF's nurses did follow protocol actions). TIM-HF2's benefit grew with distance to a cardiologist, 13% lower risk per doubling of distance [D1-01-F31]. The TELE-HF authors stressed "a thorough, independent evaluation of disease-management strategies before their adoption" [D1-01-F32].
130	
131	**Pooled analyses, which conflict.** A 2026 meta-analysis of 79 trials (31,669 patients) found remote monitoring cut heart-failure admissions (IRR 0.81) and death (RR 0.90) with no difference by method [D1-01-F53]. Another 2026 meta-analysis of 16 trials (8,618) found a gradient: pressure-guided RR 0.71, structured remote management 0.79, non-invasive telemonitoring alone 0.93, not significant; the authors wrote "passive telemonitoring alone is insufficient" [D1-01-F54]. They used different trial sets [D1-01-F54].
132	
133	**The Indian treatment gap.** In the Trivandrum registry (1,205 admissions, 16 hospitals, Kerala, 2013), only 25% of patients with weak pumping were discharged on all three drug classes, and 5-year mortality was 59% [D1-01-F35]. The national registry (10,851 patients, 53 hospitals) found 47.5% of eligible patients on guideline drugs, 90-day mortality 14.2% [D1-01-F47] and 1-year 22.1% [D1-01-F48]. A second registry (5,182 patients) found adherence to all three classes of 18.8% in men and 15.9% in women; one registry counts prescriptions, the other adherence [D1-01-F49]. After a heart attack with weak pumping, use of one class (MRA) fell from 69% to 6% within a year [D1-01-F50]. The registries report drug classes, not dose levels [D1-01-F35, D1-01-F47].
134	
135	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: heart failure fits the challenge's "far from a specialist" best, but the working loop needs lab values and visits, so it belongs on the roadmap, not in tonight's build.
136	
137	### Other conditions, briefly
138	
139	The other conditions repeat the pattern and add two lessons: a dose loop can work with no sensor at all, and rehabilitation by software matches in-person care without beating usual care.
140	
141	- **Warfarin.** A Cochrane review of 28 trials (8,950 patients) found that patients who tested INR at home and adjusted their own dose by a schedule had fewer clots (RR 0.47) and lower death (RR 0.55). Patients who tested at home and left the dose to the clinic had fewer clots (RR 0.69) but no change in death (RR 0.94). Each approach was compared with usual care in separate sets of trials, not with each other. Major bleeding did not change overall (RR 0.95) [D1-02-F05].
142	- **Gout.** In a UK trial (517 patients, Nottingham, 2 years), nurses titrating urate-lowering drugs to a target reached it in 95% against 30% under GP care, RR 3.18, at £5,066 per quality-adjusted life year. It was not digital: it was a protocol run by nurses [D1-02-F06].
143	- **Asthma and COPD.** SMART (one inhaler for both maintenance and relief, so each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose) cut exacerbations by RR 0.68 in 16 trials with 22,748 people aged 12 and over [D1-02-F37]. No sensor was needed because the patient's own reliever use is the signal and the inhaler delivers the dose change at that moment. Sensor inhalers did less: reminders raised adherence without changing school absence [D1-02-F01]; the Digihaler system's benefit interval crossed 1 and adherence fell from 79.2% to 68.6% over 6 months [D1-02-F02]; a Propeller trial cut reliever use but not asthma control scores overall (company-affiliated authors) [D1-02-F38]. Commercially, Teva withdrew the Digihaler app and US inhalers on 1 June 2024 [D1-02-F41], and an undated ResMed page says Propeller "has ceased operations" [D1-02-F40].
144	- **Rehabilitation by software.** Stroke telerehab after discharge was no better than usual care for daily-living activities (SMD 0.00) and about equal to in-person physiotherapy [D1-02-F07]. Lung telerehab, 99% COPD, matched centre rehab on walking distance, with completion 93% against 70% [D1-02-F03]. A Sword Health trial (140 back-pain patients, company-affiliated) found no difference in disability against in-person physiotherapy but lower dropout, 15.7% against 34.3% [D1-02-F08]. PHTI (June 2024) found physiotherapist-guided virtual care comparable to in-person care with lower spending, app-only exercise "unlikely to be effective as total substitutes", and did not separate the effect of adapting exercise to measured performance [D1-02-F54].
145	- **Biofeedback and stimulation.** Device-guided breathing lowered systolic BP by 3.67 mmHg across 8 trials, but showed no effect once the 5 manufacturer-linked trials were removed [D1-02-F11]. Nerivio, a sham-controlled migraine stimulator, gave pain relief at 2 hours in 66.7% against 38.8%, but it uses no sensor loop [D1-02-F12].
146	
147	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: a sensor earns its place only if it changes a decision that a cheaper signal cannot. Warfarin and SMART show the dose rule itself carries the benefit.

168	### Drop-off and adherence technology
169	
170	People stop using health apps quickly, and the trials show that raising adherence on its own often leaves outcomes unchanged.
171	
172	**Retention.**
173	- 93 Android mental-health apps with 10,000 or more installs (2019): the median app kept 3.3% of users at day 30 [D1-02-F26].
174	- Eight remote US studies, over 100,000 people: median retention 5.5 days; referral by a clinician added 40 days, payment 22 days (one study) [D1-02-F27].
175	- Chronic-disease app trials: pooled dropout 43% (40% in randomised trials, 49% in observational studies) [D1-02-F28].
176	- Engagement strategies helped modestly, SMD 0.33, very low certainty [D1-02-F56].
177	- With a clinician in the loop, retention was higher: Sword dropout 15.7% [D1-02-F08]; lung telerehab completion 93% [D1-02-F03].
178	
179	**Adherence rose; outcomes did not.**
180	
181	| Trial | Patients | Adherence result | Outcome result |
182	|---|---|---|---|
183	| Inhaler reminders, New Zealand, 2015 | 220 children, 6 months | 84% against 30% | School absence 1.9% against 1.7%, no difference [D1-02-F01] |
184	| MedISAFE-BP reminder app, US, 2018 | 411 adults, 12 weeks | Adherence score +0.4 | Systolic -0.5 mmHg, p=0.78 [D1-01-F06] |

197	| Blood pressure | TASMINH2 | Leg swelling 32% against 22% (p=0.022); other side effects similar [D1-01-F01] |
198	| Blood pressure | TASMIN-SR | "without excessive adverse events" [D1-01-F02] |
199	| Blood pressure | TASMINH4 | Adverse events similar in all arms [D1-01-F03] |
200	| Blood pressure | CRHCP, 18 months | No treatment-related serious adverse events [D1-01-F09] |
201	| Blood pressure | CRHCP, 4 years | No difference in injurious falls, symptomatic low BP, fainting or kidney outcomes [D1-01-F38] |
202	| Insulin | d-Nav | Low blood sugar 0.29 against 0.29 events a month [D1-01-F13] |
203	| Insulin | TeleDiab-2 | No severe low blood sugar; mild episodes similar [D1-01-F14] |
204	| Insulin | My Dose Coach, no control | Low blood sugar in 12-16% of US users [D1-01-F15], 1.4% in the Gulf [D1-01-F16] |
205	| Closed loop | Control-IQ; iLet | Time below 70 mg/dL fell; 1 diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA, a dangerous acid build-up) [D1-01-F24]. Severe low blood sugar 17.7 against 10.8 per 100 patient-years, not significant [D1-01-F25] |
206	| Closed loop, type 2 | CamAPS HX; 2IQP; twiist | 1 serious adverse event [D1-01-F26]; 1 severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F43]; 1 DKA, no control arm [D1-01-F44] |
207	| Heart failure | STRONG-HF | Any adverse event by day 90: 41% against 29%; serious 16% against 17%; fatal 5% against 6% [D1-01-F27]; similar by age [D1-01-F28] |
208	| Heart failure | Chatbot titration, Russia | Potassium and kidney function no different at 6 weeks [D1-01-F51] |
209	
210	Not in the notes: potassium and kidney event rates by arm in STRONG-HF (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
211	
212	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: protocol titration has a good safety record when the protocol has stop rules. The known costs are more minor side effects, leg swelling in self-managed BP care, and low blood sugar with insulin, so each needs its own safety branch.
213	
214	### What a doctor in a small town would ask
215	
216	OUR VIEW. These are the questions we expect, with what the evidence can and cannot answer.
217	
218	1. **Time saved.** A primary-care consultation in India lasted about 2 minutes in 2013-2015 [D1-03-F24], and 79.9% of required posts in four specialities (surgeon, physician, obstetrician-gynaecologist, paediatrician) in rural community health centres were unfilled in March 2023 [D1-03-F16]. A product that adds screens to the visit repeats mWellcare [D1-01-F46]. It must do the reading, the protocol logic and the draft, and leave one approve-or-change action. How long approval takes in practice: NOT RESEARCHED.
219	2. **Which protocol.** Doctors will trust a protocol they already use. Trials that worked used pre-agreed plans or standard protocols [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F09]; an Indian state protocol with steps, thresholds and 30-day re-checks already exists [D1-06-F14].
220	3. **Can I overrule it.** In every positive BP trial a named person held the authority: patient by a pre-agreed plan, GP, pharmacist or supervised village doctor [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F03, D1-01-F04, D1-01-F09]. The design must let the doctor change or refuse any proposal, and record why.
221	4. **Are home readings valid.** Home and clinic targets differ (TASMIN-SR used a home target of 120/75) [D1-01-F02]; reading rules are in part E.
222	5. **Who is liable** if a proposed step harms a patient, and what licence the tool needs. The notes in this part cannot answer this; see part F2.
223	6. **Who pays me** for the time. Not answerable here; see part F2.
224	
225	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: a doctor will judge the product on minutes and liability before outcomes.
226	
227	### What we could not find
228	
229	- An Indian randomised trial of home BP readings driving a titration protocol (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
230	- Potassium and kidney rates by arm in STRONG-HF; GOALS-HF results [D1-01-F52].
231	- PHTI's category-level mmHg figures for hypertension (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
232	- Dose levels in any Indian heart-failure registry [D1-01-F35].
233	- Rejoyn's primary publication and sales [D1-02-F49].
234	- Indian evidence for warfarin, gout, asthma or rehab loops (D1-02, NOT SEARCHED list).
235	- Only the facts the claims checks (D3-01, D3-02) reached have been re-verified; their corrections are applied here.
236	
237	### So what for us
238	
239	OUR VIEW.
240	- Build at adaptive depth 4: the reading must come back as a proposed dose change, or we sit with the null trials [D1-01-F05, D1-01-F39].
241	- Give the decision to a named person under a written protocol, and make approving it take seconds; electronics added little once someone titrated [D1-01-F03, D1-01-F09].
242	- Aim at the gap mWellcare left: between visits and among the 49% who do not return [D1-01-F46, D1-03-F10].
243	- Treat adherence as an input to the dose rule, never as the product [D1-02-F59, D1-01-F06].
244	- Write a safety branch for each known harm (swelling, low BP, falls, kidney, low sugar) and report it from day one [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F38].
245

1	## D2. How care has been scaled without specialists
2	
3	### What this part shows
4	
5	India and other low-income settings have raised blood-pressure control without specialists by giving routine work to nurses and health workers under a written protocol, backed by free drugs and regular refills. In India the dose change still waits for a doctor's visit, and that is where a home step loop could fit.
6	
7	### India's hypertension programme in practice
8	
9	The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) shows what a protocol programme does well, and where patients drop out.
10	
11	**Design choices**
12	- A protocol of 3 to 4 steps, amlodipine first. Punjab: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg (to 80 mg), then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (to 25 mg). Maharashtra orders the steps differently [D3-05-F01].
13	- Free drugs, given as 30-day refills at every facility level from health and wellness centres (HWC) to district hospitals; sub-centres are not named [D3-05-F02].
14	- The open-source Simple app: about 80 seconds to register a patient, 15 seconds for a follow-up, overdue lists with high-risk patients first, one-click nurse calls, automated reminders [D3-05-F03].
15	
16	**Who does what.** Medical officers start amlodipine and review at 30 days; nurses register patients and record follow-up; Senior Treatment Supervisors support training. Who steps the dose in Maharashtra is not stated [D3-05-F06].
17	
18	**Starts and losses.** Two cohorts give different loss figures; they differ in sites, years and definition:
19	
20	| Cohort | Started | Not seen again | Control among those seen |
21	|---|---|---|---|
22	| 24 sentinel sites, 4 states, registered 2018-19 | 21,895 | 49% (51% returned by Jul-Sep 2019) | 26.3% at registration, 59.8% at follow-up [D1-03-F10] |
23	| Punjab and Maharashtra, started 2018-2021 | 281,209 | 36% (no visit Jan-Mar 2022) | 70% and 76% on amlodipine 5 mg alone; 75% and 81% after step 2 [D3-05-F04] |
24	
25	District surveys found 14.5% of people with hypertension controlled in 2018-19 and 21.2% in 2023-24, with no control districts [D1-01-F10, D1-01-F11]. The programme's own deck claims 75 million people with hypertension and/or diabetes on standard care by December 2025 (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F10].
26	
27	**Why patients stopped.** A Bathinda (Punjab) phone survey of 157 people who had missed visits for over 3 months, a small convenience sample: no sense of being ill 24.8%, distance 22.2%, no guidance or reminder 15.2%, acute illness 8.2% [D3-05-F07].
28	
29	**The refill rule.** A doctor dispenses the first medicine. Trained paramedical staff dispense the monthly refill only when pressure is controlled; uncontrolled patients are sent to a doctor for a dose change [D3-05-F08].
30	
31	**Cost.** Amlodipine for the first two steps cut drug cost about 20%, from US$2.50 to US$2.05 per patient per year [D3-05-F05]. A 2022 WHO release gives "as low as Rs 200" per patient per year, a modelled drug cost (SOURCE ESTIMATE) [D3-05-F09]. Neither includes staff; a full cost was not found.
32	
33	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: IHCI already has the protocol, free drugs, a record and an overdue list. It lacks a dose decision for the uncontrolled patient who does not go back to the doctor.
34	
35	### Who may change a dose in India
36	
37	- Opened source: in Bathinda, paramedical staff refill only when pressure is controlled; uncontrolled patients go to a doctor [D3-05-F08].
38	- Search summary only: state protocol text has the medical officer start and raise the dose; once controlled, the ANM (auxiliary nurse midwife) at the HWC or sub-centre measures pressure and gives a month's medicines [D3-05-F31].
39	- Search summary only: community health officer (CHO) duties are screening, referral and follow-up; starting treatment sits with the medical officer and staff nurse [D3-05-F30, D3-05-F13].
40	- NOT FOUND: any order letting a CHO or nurse start or change an antihypertensive dose. The 2023-2030 national NCD guidelines could not be opened.
41	
42	We cannot say they may, nor that they are barred. It remains a question for state health departments and a lawyer.
43	
44	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: design for a doctor approving every dose change.
45	
46	### Tamil Nadu's doorstep scheme
47	
48	Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam (MTM) brings screening and medicines to the home [D3-05-F15].
49	- Scale: launched August 2021; by August 2024, 1,86,13,872 beneficiaries, with 92,59,821 people with hypertension given medicines (government figures, not audited; THEIR CLAIM) [D3-05-F14].
50	- Women health volunteers deliver drugs to registered patients over 45 or with poor mobility (search summary only) [D3-05-F16].
51	- A 2025 survey of 6,856 adults: over 95% of those diagnosed on treatment, but a hypertension control rate of only 35.4% (the abstract does not state the denominator) [D1-03-F09].
52	- **It refills; it does not step.** No source says the dose is changed at the door; delivery continues the existing prescription [D3-05-F15].
53	
54	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the drugs already reach the door at the same dose; high treatment with low control is the gap a dose step addresses.
55	
56	### Programmes outside India
57	
58	| Programme, size | Who decides the dose | Who delivers | Also in the package | Result | Comparison group |
59	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
60	| China rural project; 326 villages, 33,995 | Village doctors by protocol, physician-supervised | Village doctors | Free or discounted drugs; doctors paid on control rate; audit; free home cuffs (search summary only) | Under 130/80 at 18 months 57.0% vs 19.9%; 4-year events HR 0.75 (60+), 0.64 (under 60); no rise in falls | Yes, cluster trial [D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38, D3-05-F21] |
61	| Lesotho; 103 villages, 547 | Lay village health workers, by app | Same workers | One fixed-dose pill | Under 140/90 at 12 months 58% vs 48%, p=0.046 | Yes, cluster trial vs facility referral [D3-05-F24] |
62	| IMPACT-BP, South Africa; 774 | Nurses remotely by app (not stated explicitly) | Health worker at home collects readings, delivers medicine | Home cuff | Systolic 7.9-9.1 mmHg lower at 6 months; control 57.6% vs 76.9-82.8% (ACC summary) or about 32% vs 60% (GroundUp, time point not stated) | Yes, vs standard care [D3-05-F27] |
63	| Nigeria; 60 centres, 21,922 | Health workers under standing orders (search summary only) | Centre staff | Free drugs, then US$1.60 co-pay a month; single pills 16.3% to 65.2%; 30-day stock 27% to 96% of centres | Control 21.7% to 55.9% (2020-2023) | No [D3-05-F22, D3-05-F23] |
64	| Uganda HIV clinic; 1,082 | Clinic | Clinic | 3-month refills once controlled | Control 73.5% to 78.3%; 96.4% retained | No [D3-05-F36] |
65	| COBRA-BPS, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka; 2,645 | Trained physicians; health workers did not change doses | Health worker home visits | Counselling, coordination | Systolic 5.2 mmHg lower at 24 months | Yes, cluster trial [D1-01-F37] |
66	| CARRS, India and Pakistan; 1,146 | Physicians, with software prompts | Care coordinators calling monthly | Low-cost generics | Combined target 18.2% vs 8.7%; more mild lows | Yes, 28 months [D3-05-F18] |
67	| mWellcare, India; 3,698 | Nurse-managed care, app prompts | Nurses | Reminders | Systolic difference 0.98 mmHg (CI -4.64 to 2.67): null | Yes, 12 months [D1-01-F46] |
68	| Kaiser, US (search summary only) | Not stated | Medical assistants | Registry, single pill | Control 43.6% (2001) to 80.4% (2009) | No [D3-05-F20] |
69	| PAHO HEARTS, 33 countries | Roadmap names nurse dose adjustment | Primary care | Multi-month prescriptions | About 60% where fully run (THEIR CLAIM) | No [D3-05-F28] |
70	
71	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the largest controlled gains came where a non-doctor could step the dose, with free drugs or one pill; monitoring, counselling or prompts gained less or nothing.
72	
73	### What the fixes are worth
74	
75	| Fix | Evidence |
76	|---|---|
77	| Longer refills | Uganda 3-month refills: 96.4% retained, control 73.5% to 78.3%, no control group [D3-05-F36] |
78	| Single-pill combinations | Systolic 3.99 mmHg lower at week 12 vs separate pills; mostly observational (search summary only) [D3-05-F39] |
79	| Home delivery | IMPACT-BP home arm 7.9 mmHg lower [D3-05-F27] |
80	| Phone follow-up | Calls beat generic reminders, "moderately effective" (search summary only) [D3-05-F41]; no Indian trial isolates calls |
81	
82	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: each fix keeps patients on drugs; none changes the dose.
83	
84	### What these programmes changed that software alone could not
85	
86	- Drug stock: Nigeria [D3-05-F22]; IHCI [D3-05-F02]; China [D1-01-F38].
87	- Authority for a non-doctor to change drugs: China [D1-01-F09]; Lesotho [D3-05-F24]; PAHO roadmap [D3-05-F28].
88	- A person carrying medicine to the home: IMPACT-BP [D3-05-F27]; Tamil Nadu [D3-05-F14].
89	- Pay linked to control and physician audit: China [D3-05-F21].
90	- A person who phones and books visits: CARRS [D3-05-F18]; IHCI nurses [D3-05-F03].
91	- Software alone, mWellcare, added nothing [D1-01-F46].
92	
93	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: software was part of every working programme and the whole of none.
94	
95	### Where a home step loop fits (OUR VIEW)
96	
97	**What it adds to IHCI today**
98	- The dose step for patients who do not return (36-49% [D3-05-F04, D1-03-F10]), who now need a doctor's visit to step up [D3-05-F08]. The loop sends the doctor a proposed step from home readings, approved without a visit.
99	- A reading trusted enough to act on, so the "controlled or not" rule [D3-05-F08] can run at home.
100	- It answers distance and missing guidance, not "no sense of being ill" [D3-05-F07].
101	
102	**What it must borrow:** free 30-day refills [D3-05-F02] or doorstep delivery [D3-05-F14]; a person who follows up [D3-05-F03]; the protocol [D3-05-F01]; a doctor's sign-off [D3-05-F30].
103	
104	**Closest precedent:** IMPACT-BP, with home cuffs, delivered medicine and remote nurse decisions [D3-05-F27]. Warnings: visit-time prompts added nothing [D1-01-F46], and China's gain came with drugs and incentives [D1-01-F38].
105	
106	### What we could not find
107	
108	- Any order letting a CHO or nurse change a dose; the national NCD guidelines text.
109	- IHCI full cost per patient; Maharashtra's titrator; an effect size for nurse calls.
110	- Tamil Nadu's delivering cadre and refill interval; who exactly changed doses in IMPACT-BP; Kerala control outcomes.
111	- An Indian decentralised-refill pilot with numbers; China's programme cost; INTE-COMM results; an ECHO India effect on control [D3-05-F33].
112

## Appendix A. The challenge, the burden and the voices in detail

This appendix holds the detail behind chapter 1: what the fund's challenge asks a product to do (A1 to A3), how many people in India it concerns and how few are controlled (A4 to A8), why care breaks down between visits (A9 to A12), and what patients and doctors say in public (A13). The trials behind the challenge's demands are in Appendix B.

### A1. The challenge, phrase by phrase

This section turns each phrase of the fund's challenge into what a product must do. The middle column is our reading of each phrase. Terms are explained in A15.

| The fund's words | What a product must do (OUR VIEW) | Facts behind it |
|---|---|---|
| "rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers" | A signal that moves within days of a treatment change and is cheap and correct to measure at home. | Bluetooth cuff: about ₹2,500-2,900 (online listings, mid-2026 or undated; search summary only) [D1-06-F31]. Signal speeds: Appendix B3. |
| "continuously personalise care" | Recompute the treatment from this patient's readings: protocol step, response to the last step, medicine taken or not, what is unsafe. | Gujarat's hypertension sheet: "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" [D1-06-F14]. |
| "adaptive to patient needs between appointments" | Change the treatment without waiting for the next visit. | 51% of 21,895 patients at 24 government hypertension programme sites returned for follow-up (A6) [D1-03-F10]. |
| "measurable improvements in health outcomes" | One endpoint that can move in 90 days, with an accepted threshold for "clinically meaningful" (A3). | An independent US review (October 2024) set it at 5 mmHg of systolic pressure (the upper number) [D1-01-F39]. |
| "patients who cannot access frequent specialist support" | Move the routine decision to a general doctor, nurse or health worker under a written protocol. The specialist owns the protocol and sees the exceptions. | 79.9% of required specialist posts at rural community health centres were unfilled (A9) [D1-03-F16]. |
| "beyond monitoring and reminders" | Reach adaptive depth 4: the therapy itself changes (A2). | Self-monitoring alone: 1.0 mmHg; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or lifestyle counselling): 6.1 (Appendix B4) [D1-01-F05]. |

### A2. What "beyond monitoring and reminders" rules in and out

This document scores every product on an "adaptive depth" scale from 0 to 4. The fund names levels 1 and 2. OUR VIEW: it is asking for level 4.

| Level | Examples in the notes | What the evidence shows |
|---|---|---|
| 0: uses no patient data | Nerivio migraine wearable, switched on by the patient, rated 0-1 [D1-02-F12]. India: none rated 0 | Nothing adapts. |
| 1: shows data | India: pocket ECGs (search summary only) [D1-04-F32]. Abroad: Omron VitalSight [D1-01-F39] | Self-monitoring alone: no effect [D1-01-F05]; one exception, a glucose sensor (Appendix B5) [D1-01-F42]. |
| 2: reminders, generic content | India: government Simple app, with overdue lists and reminder messages [D3-05-F03]. Abroad: Medisafe reminder app | Medisafe reminder app against control: 0.5 mmHg, not significant (Appendix B9) [D1-01-F06]. |
| 3: coaching from the person's own data | India: Sugar.fit, BeatO, Fitterfly [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. Abroad: CureApp HT, Japan | CureApp HT against lifestyle advice alone: 24-hour systolic 2.4 mmHg lower (Appendix B4) [D1-01-F07]. |
| 4: changes the therapy (dose, protocol step, exercise prescription) | India: only Sanofi's My Dose Coach found, its Indian results unconfirmed [D1-04-F09]. Abroad: d-Nav; insulin pumps [D1-05-F41] | d-Nav dose device against clinician support alone: HbA1c (three-month average sugar) down 1.0 point against 0.3 (Appendix B5) [D1-01-F13]. |

**The line between 3 and 4.** Level 3 changes the advice: what to eat, how to exercise. Level 4 changes the prescription: a new dose or protocol step. A clinician approving each change keeps it at level 4. Indian diabetes programmes sit at 3: no page says sensor data changes a drug dose [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. The test: after the software runs, the prescription is different.

The loop that level 4 needs (sense, decide, confirm, act, learn) is set out in Appendix B1 (picture in chapter 1).

### A3. What "measurable" means

One endpoint per condition that a pilot could read at about 90 days. The trials behind each effect are described in full in Appendix B.

| Condition | Endpoint | Effect the trials found | "Clinically meaningful" threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| High blood pressure | Share under 140/90 [D1-06-F03] | 57.2% controlled with pharmacist dose changes from home readings, against 30.0% with usual care (Appendix B4) [D1-01-F04] | 5 mmHg systolic against usual care [D1-01-F39] |
| Type 2 diabetes on insulin | HbA1c | Down 1.44-1.48 points with daily dose proposals, against 0.92 with standard care (Appendix B5) [D1-01-F14] | None given; a US review judged 0.23-0.60 points not meaningful for type 2 tools without a continuous sensor [D1-05-F04] |
| Diabetes with a sensor | Time in range | Up 14 points with a dose algorithm (Appendix B5) [D1-01-F43] | NOT RESEARCHED |
| Heart failure | Readmission or death | 15.2% against 23.3% at 180 days with fast dose stepping after discharge, adjusted estimates (Appendix B6) [D1-01-F27] | NOT RESEARCHED |
| Warfarin | Time in the target INR range | Trials against usual care report clots (risk ratio 0.47) and deaths (0.55) instead (Appendix B7) [D1-02-F05] | NOT RESEARCHED |

No blood-pressure dose-change trial in our first-round notes reported before 6 months [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F04].

### A4. How many people

The surveys measure different ages, use different blood-pressure rules and ran in different years, so they disagree. We give each figure with its source and do not pick one.

| Condition | Figure | Year of data | Who was counted | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High blood pressure | 35.5% | 2008-2020 | ICMR-INDIAB, adults 20+, measured BP, 113,043 people, 31 states and union territories | [D1-03-F01] |
| High blood pressure | 315 million people, a 2021 projection by the survey's investigators, not a count in the paper | 2008-2020 survey, projected to 2021 | Same study, investigators' commentary and press | [D1-03-F02] |
| High blood pressure | 22.6%; 24% of men, 21% of women (search summary only) | 2019-21 | NFHS-5 (National Family Health Survey), ages 15+ | [D1-03-F03, D1-03-F04] |
| High blood pressure | 45.9% | 2017-19 | LASI (Longitudinal Ageing Study in India), adults 45+, 72,262 people | [D1-03-F25] |
| High blood pressure | 22.1% of men, 19.4% of women, elevated or on drugs (search summary only, provisional) | 2023-24 | NFHS-6 | [D1-03-F22] |
| Diabetes | 11.4%; prediabetes 15.3% | 2008-2020 | ICMR-INDIAB, adults 20+ | [D1-03-F01] |
| Diabetes | 101 million; prediabetes 136 million, 2021 projections by the survey's investigators, not counts in the paper | 2008-2020 survey, projected to 2021 | Same study, investigators' commentary and press | [D1-03-F02] |
| Diabetes | 89.8 million (age-standardised 10.5%); 156.7 million projected for 2050 | 2024 | IDF Diabetes Atlas, adults 20-79 | [D1-03-F28] |
| Diabetes | 20.9% of men, 17.8% of women with high sugar or on drugs, against 15.6% and 13.5% in NFHS-5 (search summary only, provisional) | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, random glucose (a screening test) | [D1-03-F22] |
| COPD (chronic lung disease); asthma | 55.3 million; 37.9 million (search summary only) | 2016 | GBD state study | [D1-03-F36] |
| Chronic kidney disease | 13.24% pooled; an older review 3-4% by a different method (search summary only) | 2011-2023 | Community studies | [D1-03-F37] |
| Heart failure | 1.3-4.6 million cases, or about 8-10 million; the estimates differ (see A7) | 2010; 2016 | Reviews built from local and disease-specific data, no national survey | [D3-07-F24, D3-07-F25] |

Why they differ, as the notes give it:
- **Blood pressure, 35.5% against 22.6%.** Different ages (20+ against 15+), years and use of the BP threshold [D1-03-F01, D1-03-F04]. LASI counts only people 45+ [D1-03-F25].
- **Diabetes, 101 million against 89.8 million.** Different survey base and age definition; the 101 million is a 2021 projection of survey rates [D1-03-F02, D1-03-F28].
- **NFHS-6.** Random glucose is a screening test, and the findings are provisional [D1-03-F22].

### A5. The care cascade

(Picture in chapter 1: the share of adults with high blood pressure who know, are treated and are controlled, 2018-19 and 2023-24.)

A care cascade follows people with a condition through four steps: has it, knows it, is treated, is controlled. Percentages compare only when the denominator (the group the percentage is taken of) is the same, and several sources do not state it clearly.

#### High blood pressure

| Source | Aware or diagnosed | Treated | Controlled | Denominator | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NFHS-5 district paper, 2019-21 [D1-03-F05] | 46.0% (district average; range 6.1-89.6%) | 18.7% | Not used: the abstract gives 32.9% "of individuals with hypertension", which cannot sit above 18.7% treated; the preprint below gives 9.1% of all for the same 2019-21 survey [D1-03-F07] | Contested; do not read this row as one chain | Abstract opened |
| NFHS-5 preprint, 1.69 million adults, 2019-21 [D1-03-F07] | 36.7% (about 1 in 3) | 17.7% (under 1 in 5) | 9.1% (about 1 in 11) | All people with hypertension | Preprint; record opened |
| NFHS-5 and NFHS-4, ages 15-49 (Cureus 2023) [D1-03-F06] | | | 73.7% (80.8% in NFHS-4) | Only people on BP drugs, ages 15-49 | Abstract opened |
| LASI, adults 45+, 2017-19 [D1-03-F25] | 55.7% | 38.9% | 31.7% | All hypertensives for the first two; **control denominator not stated, check before use** | Abstract opened |
| LASI, self-reported [D1-03-F26] | 4 in 10 not aware | 73% of the aware | 10% of the treated | Changes at each step | Search summary only |

The same survey gives 73.7% controlled when only people aged 15-49 on drugs are counted, and 9.1% (about 1 in 11) when everyone with hypertension is counted; the ages and denominators differ, so the two do not compare [D1-03-F06, D1-03-F07]. A LASI preprint found 63.8% of measured hypertension undiagnosed, about 46 million older Indians (search summary only) [D1-03-F27].

**The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) district surveys.** The government programme surveyed the same 9 districts in 5 states twice. The surveys are before and after, with no comparison districts [D1-01-F10, D1-01-F11, D1-03-F12]. The 2018-19 source was opened.

| | 2018-19 | 2023-24 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| People with hypertension | 7,047 [D1-01-F10] | 7,324 [D1-01-F11] | |
| Aware | 52.4% [D1-01-F10] | 58.5% [D1-03-F12] | +6.1 points (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
| Treated | 40.8% [D1-01-F10] | 44.7% [D1-03-F12] | +3.9 points (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
| Controlled | 14.5% [D1-01-F10] | 21.2% [D1-01-F11] | +6.7 points [D1-03-F12] |

In 2018-19, control was under 5% in two of the districts [D1-01-F10].

#### Diabetes

- **Undiagnosed:** 43%, about 38.6 million, in 2024 [D1-03-F28].
- **Treated but not controlled:** in Tamil Nadu over 95% of diagnosed people were treated, yet the diabetes control rate was 9.8% (the abstract does not state the denominator; survey detail in A6) [D1-03-F09].
- **Slow insulin starts:** a mean of 7 years of diabetes before insulin in one older Indian study (search summary only) [D1-03-F30]. AIIMS Bhopal clinic records (950 patients, not a trial) classed 11.8% as insulin inertia (delay in starting or raising insulin), mean HbA1c (a blood test showing average sugar over about three months) 8.43% [D1-03-F29].

### A6. Treatment is not control, and half do not return

Two Indian data sets show that getting people onto medicine is not enough, and that people who return do far better than those who do not.

**Tamil Nadu survey.** The state's doorstep programme, Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam, was surveyed in 6,856 adults aged 30+ across all 38 districts (paper abstract, 2025; a South First news report gives 6,809) [D1-03-F09]. Screening reached 79.4% for diabetes and 82.6% for hypertension, and over 95% of diagnosed people were on treatment. Control rates remained low: 9.8% for diabetes and 35.4% for hypertension; the abstract does not say whether these are shares of everyone with the disease, the diagnosed or the treated [D1-03-F09]. How the scheme delivers medicines is in Appendix B13.

**IHCI cohort.** A government programme with a fixed drug protocol. The cohort registered 21,895 patients at 24 sentinel sites in Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Telangana (Jan 2018-Jun 2019), followed up Jul-Sep 2019, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10].
- Only 11,274 (51%) returned [D1-03-F10].
- Among returners, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% [D1-03-F10].
- Control was 70.4% in primary care against 52.2% in secondary care [D1-03-F10].
- Protocol drugs: amlodipine, telmisartan or losartan, chlorthalidone or hydrochlorothiazide; 44.6% were on amlodipine 5 mg alone at follow-up [D1-03-F11].

A second IHCI cohort, in Punjab and Maharashtra, gives a different loss figure; the two are compared in Appendix B11.

**Return visits.** About 27% of registered IHCI patients did not return in Jan-Mar 2021 (search summary only) [D1-03-F13]. IHCI enrolled about 4 million patients, about 12.5% of the estimated total, by around 2022 (search summary only) [D1-03-F13]. Pooled Indian non-adherence to BP drugs is 48%, with a prediction interval of 9-90% (search summary only) [D1-03-F44]. The reasons patients give for missing visits are in A13.

### A7. Heart failure and stroke in India

No national count of heart failure was found, and the estimates differ widely: 1.3 to 4.6 million cases in a 2010 estimate built from disease-specific figures, whose authors say no surveillance exists (quoted in a 2024 review) [D3-07-F24], against about 8 to 10 million, about 1% of the population, in a 2016 review of local and global studies (search summary only) [D3-07-F25]. For stroke, the Global Burden of Disease study put India's prevalent cases at 9.4 million in 2021, up from 4.4 million in 1990, with over 1.25 million new cases a year (press report quoting the authors) [D3-07-F26].

The registries show patients leave hospital on too few of the drugs that work and stop them afterwards. The three guideline classes are beta blocker, RAS blocker (ACE inhibitor or ARB) and MRA.

| Registry | Who | Treatment finding | Outcome | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Heart Failure Registry | 10,851 acute patients, 53 hospitals, 21 states | 47.5% of eligible patients on guideline drugs | 90-day mortality 14.2%; 1-year mortality 22.1% | [D1-01-F47, D1-01-F48] |
| Indian College of Cardiology registry | 5,182 acute patients, 17 centres, 2019-2021 | All three classes taken: 18.8% of men, 15.9% of women | 1-year death 18.1% | [D1-01-F49] |
| Trivandrum, Kerala | 1,205 admissions, 16 hospitals, 2013 | Only 25% of patients with weak pumping discharged on all three drug classes | 5-year mortality 59% | [D1-01-F35] |
| NORIN-STEMI, Delhi | Heart-attack patients with weak pumping | Use of one class (MRA) fell from 69% at discharge to 6% at 1 year | | [D1-01-F50] |

The national registries differ (47.5% against about 17%) partly because one counts prescription and the other adherence [D1-01-F49]. The registries report drug classes, not dose levels; none reports doses as a share of target [D1-01-F35, D1-01-F47, D1-01-F49]. The trials of dose stepping and telemonitoring in heart failure are in Appendix B6.

### A8. The world and Japan

Low control is a world problem, and Japan, the fund's home, has a large, old population with high blood pressure.

| Measure | Figure | Year | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| World hypertension (30-79) | About 1.4 billion; 44% unaware; 23% controlled; two-thirds in low- and middle-income countries | 2024 | [D1-03-F32] |
| World diabetes | 830 million adults; 59% of those 30+ not on diabetes medicine | 2022 | [D1-03-F33] |
| Japan hypertension | About 43 million; about 31 million (73%) poorly controlled (search summary only) | 2010 base, cited for 2017 | [D1-03-F47] |
| Japan aged 65+ | 29.4% (Sep 2025); 34.8% projected for 2040 (search summary only) | 2025 | [D1-03-F48] |
| Japan visit length | 10.2 minutes | 2012 | [D1-03-F24] |

### A9. The specialist and time gap

Few specialists work where most patients live, and doctors who see chronic patients have very little time per visit. This is what the challenge's phrase "patients who cannot access frequent specialist support" means in India.

**Rural community health centre (CHC) specialist posts, March 2023** [D1-03-F16]:

| Specialty | Shortfall | Share of required posts |
|---|---|---|
| Surgeon | 4,578 | 83.3% [D1-03-F16] |
| Physician | 4,499 | 81.9% [D1-03-F16] |
| Paediatrician | 4,425 | 80.5% [D1-03-F16] |
| Obstetrician-gynaecologist | 4,078 | 74.2% [D1-03-F16] |
| All four | 17,551 of 21,964 (4,413 in post) | 79.9% [D1-03-F16] |

The article's rows sum to 17,580, not 17,551 [D1-03-F16]. The shortfall has stayed near 17,500 since 2014-15 [D1-03-F17].

**Specialist counts.** The only figures are from a 2017 parliamentary committee (search summary only): about 4,000 cardiologists, 1,200 nephrologists and 650 endocrinologists, against the committee's estimated needs of 88,000, 40,000 and 28,000 [D1-03-F18]. The government told Parliament it does not hold speciality-wise doctor data (news report of the reply, 13 Apr 2025) [D3-07-F22].

**Consultation length.** Indian primary-care visits lasted about 2.3 minutes (2013, stopwatch, 412 visits) and 2 minutes (2015) [D1-03-F24]. Japan's, for comparison, lasted 10.2 minutes in 2012 (A8) [D1-03-F24].

**Doctor ratio and its caveat.** The government gave 1:811 in Rajya Sabha (about 2 Dec 2025), counting 13,88,185 allopathic doctors plus 7,51,768 AYUSH practitioners (traditional medicine) and "assuming that 80 per cent" are available [D1-03-F40]. Allopathic doctors alone give a lower ratio. OUR ARITHMETIC from the note: 13,88,185 x 0.8 = about 11.1 lakh, about 0.79 per 1,000 people if the population is about 1.4 billion (an assumption, not sourced) [D1-03-F40].

### A10. Cost and follow-up

Families pay a large share of health costs themselves, and the share rose in the latest year on record.

- **Out-of-pocket share:** 39.4% of total health expenditure in 2021-22 and 43.41% in 2022-23 (National Health Accounts released 27 May 2026, via a news report) [D1-03-F23]. In 2022-23 household spending rose by ₹26,375 crore while government spending fell by nearly ₹49,000 crore [D1-03-F23].
- **Per visit:** medicines were 61.15% of spend per outpatient spell in a Delhi report; another report says median outpatient spend is zero (search summary only) [D1-03-F49].
- **Cheaper medicines:** 18,646 Jan Aushadhi Kendras (generic medicine shops), Feb 2026, priced 50-80% below branded [D1-03-F20].
- **Diabetes spend:** about US$109.5 per person and over US$9.8 billion in total (IDF 2024) [D1-03-F28].

The cost of a chronic-care visit to the household, and how long a dose change is delayed, were not found (A14).

### A11. Public programmes and their scale

India already screens and treats at large scale through free public programmes, the channels a loop would plug into.

| Programme | Scale (date) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| National NCD screening drives | 41.5 crore screened for hypertension, 41.3 crore for diabetes (cumulative, Aug 2026) | [D1-03-F20] |
| Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (12 free services) | Over 1.86 lakh functional (Aug 2026) | [D1-03-F19] |
| NCD clinics | 770 district clinics; 6,410 at CHCs (2026) | [D1-03-F20] |
| Tamil Nadu doorstep care | Two crore beneficiaries by Dec 2024 (search summary only) | [D1-03-F46] |
| eSanjeevani teleconsultation | Over 49 crore consultations by Aug 2026; 2.4 lakh providers | [D1-03-F19] |
| ABHA digital health ID | 96.43 crore IDs; over 110 crore records linked (Aug 2026) | [D1-03-F19] |

Progress against the "75 by 25" target (75 million on standard care by 2025) is in Appendix E [D1-03-F14]. How IHCI and Tamil Nadu's scheme run in practice is in Appendix B11 and B13.

### A12. Phones and who is left out

Most Indians have a mobile connection, but rural women and older people are least likely to own a phone, and the phone is often not the patient's.

| Measure | Figure | Year | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Smartphone owners | Over 622 million (industry estimate) | 2025 | [D1-03-F41] |
| Internet users | Over 915 million, 48% women (industry estimate) | 2025 | [D1-03-F41] |
| Internet subscriptions | 1.09 billion connections, not unique people (search summary only) | Mar 2026 | [D1-03-F31] |
| Women 15-49 owning a phone | 63.6%; rural 57.4% (search summary only) | 2023-24 | [D1-03-F42] |
| Women 15-49 who own the phone they use | 54%; rural 46.6% | Not stated | [D3-04-F23] |
| Phone ownership, 15+ | Men 83.9%, women 56.2% (search summary only) | 2025 | [D1-03-F42] |
| Rural older adults near Mysore, 150 people | 50% owned a phone, few a smartphone; digital literacy 11% | Not stated | [D3-04-F56] |
| eSanjeevani users | Women 57.14%; age 60+ 16.25% (search summary only) | 2026 | [D1-03-F21] |
| Indians who spoke English | About 10.6% | 2011 | [D3-04-F57] |

The two figures for women aged 15-49 differ (63.6% owning a phone, 54% owning the phone they use); our source parts give no year for the second and no reason for the gap [D1-03-F42, D3-04-F23].

**The phone is often not the patient's.** Caregivers enable access for older adults and devices are shared (A13) [D3-04-F05]; one review moves a meter from a husband's phone to a mother's [D3-04-F25].

### A13. What patients and doctors say in public

The team has done no interviews, so this section stands in until it does. It reports published interview studies, surveys, public app reviews and posts, labelled PUBLISHED STUDY, PUBLIC REVIEW or FORUM POST. None of it is customer evidence gathered by the team; reviews are self-selected and studies were read as abstracts only.

#### Why patients miss follow-up and stop medicines

Eight Indian interview studies (PUBLISHED STUDY) name the same causes: feeling well, cost, family duties, fear of long-term drugs, traditional medicine.

| Where | People | Barriers, in the authors' words |
|---|---|---|
| Coastal Karnataka, tertiary hospital | 32 hypertensive patients lost to follow-up | "symptom-driven healthcare seeking, medication non-adherence, occupational responsibilities, and competing family priorities"; wage loss, rushed consultations [D3-04-F01] |
| Rural Tamil Nadu (Thiruvallur) | 15 adults with diabetes or hypertension | Stopping is structural, unintentional (work, travel, caregiving) or intentional, "perceived harm, symptoms or treatment need"; "Family relationships could both support and hinder medication-taking" [D3-04-F02] |
| Tehri, Uttarakhand | 40 (20 diabetes, 20 hypertension) | "the use of alternative medicine"; "lack of self-management guidance from their physicians" [D3-04-F03] |
| West Garo Hills, Meghalaya | 52 (providers, health workers, community) | "concern about long-term treatment"; "a preference for traditional medicine constrained screening efforts"; elders decide [D3-04-F12, D3-04-F48] |
| Rural Meghalaya | 29 women aged 60+ with diabetes | "caregiving roles as barriers to care"; "feelings of guilt due to financial dependency" [D3-04-F04] |
| Rural Punjab | 8 focus groups plus 15 health professionals | "beliefs in alternative therapies, drug side effects"; "Physicians' guidance and support were motivating them" [D3-04-F13] |
| Ludhiana, urban health centre | 40 with diabetes | "side effects of taking medications daily"; "about 50% patients were adherent" [D3-04-F14] |
| Chennai and Chunampet | 54 (patients, caregivers, providers, officials) | Caregivers enable access for older adults; "shared device ownership"; "data privacy, security, and app reliability affected trust" [D3-04-F05] |

Karnataka patients suggested reminders and digital records [D3-04-F01]. A FORUM POST by an adult child says the father's pressure stayed controlled on Ayurvedic treatment, then rose, and he "re-started some medication" [D3-04-F52].

The same reasons appear in numbers in one IHCI district. A Bathinda (Punjab) phone survey of 157 people who had missed visits for over 3 months, a small convenience sample, found: no sense of being ill 24.8%, distance 22.2%, no guidance or reminder 15.2%, acute illness 8.2% [D3-05-F07].

#### Home monitors in Indian homes

Few patients own a home cuff, most taught themselves, and home readings show that many "controlled" patients are not.

- **Who has one.** Of 2,588 clinic-attending people with hypertension and caregivers in North India, 18.1% used a home monitor (urban 20.5%, rural 8.5%) [D3-04-F06]. No household figure exists; a web claim of under 5% cites no source [D3-04-F22].
- **Who taught them.** 75.2% reported "learning HBPM themselves through observation, videos, and reading"; 24.7% were trained by a health worker. Technique was excellent in 15.9% of patients and 5.9% of caregivers [D3-04-F06].
- **Do doctors act on home readings.** About 88% of 832 Indian doctors recommend home monitoring, but estimate only 30.4% of patients measure; 31.3% say to measure before tablets, about 30% give no instructions [D3-04-F07]. Only 15.1% knew the correct home thresholds [D3-04-F18].
- **What home readings reveal.** In GRAND (18 centres, 12 states, 1,920 treated regular attenders, 7 days of home readings), 77.7% looked controlled by clinic pressure but 55.9% by clinic plus home; 21.8% had masked uncontrolled pressure (high at home, normal in clinic) [D3-04-F09]. Median knowledge of home monitoring was 1 out of 7 [D3-04-F10].

#### What doctors and health workers say

Doctors describe heavy workloads, and many private doctors do not follow the state protocol.

- **Workload.** In Kolar, Karnataka: "Doctors face very high workloads, especially in the public sector"; care is "very doctor-centred" [D3-04-F16]. Meghalaya reports staff vacancies and limited training [D3-04-F12, D3-04-F20].
- **The state protocol.** Of 30 private doctors in Bhopal, 19 did not follow it, citing "fear of either losing patients due to a lack of immediate blood pressure control or causing drug-related adverse effects" and a preference for fixed-dose combinations (two drugs in one tablet) [D3-04-F15].
- **Health workers with a decision tool.** IMPACT Diabetes, a cluster trial in 16 villages in two states (418 people, 9 months): ASHAs (village health workers) with a tablet tool under physician supervision, against usual care. HbA1c fell by 0.5 or more in 21.8% against 10.3%; physician visits 85.0% against 29.8%; "acceptable and feasible for patients, ASHAs, and physicians" [D3-04-F17]. Diabetes, not blood pressure.

No Indian doctor, nurse or health worker was found speaking about dose steps from home readings (A14).

#### What users say about existing programmes

The latest 100 Apple App Store India reviews each of three diabetes programmes, BeatO, Sugar.fit and Fitterfly, were read on 13 Nov 2026. One-star reviews: 55, 76 and 9 (count from the research note's method section); Fitterfly's 5-star profile looks prompted (the note's inference). All quotes are PUBLIC REVIEW, verbatim.

| Theme | Quote 1 | Quote 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Spam calls | "Please stop calling and sending WhatsApp messages about webinar. I never signed up for it." (Sugar.fit, 17 Oct 2026) [D3-04-F27] | "we will get continuous pre recorded calls to join sugarfit class everyday atleast 5 calls." (Sugar.fit, 26 Jul 2026) [D3-04-F28] |
| No reachable person | "Since 5 days I am trying for doctor appointment but no slot available" (Sugar.fit, 21 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F30] | "Unable to access blood reports and unable to reach any support or helpline number." (Sugar.fit, 12 Oct 2026) [D3-04-F29] |
| Coaching runs dry | "by the third month, there is hardly anything new to discuss." (Sugar.fit, 26 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F33] | "no results no calling or follow ups aftee 1 month" (Sugar.fit, 25 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F34] |
| Device and data | "sensor got activated, but data never synced." (BeatO, 2 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F36] | "Within five minutes, I got five readings with a difference of over 50." (BeatO, 17 Mar 2026) [D3-04-F37] |
| Money and medicine | "Sugar.fit took ₹18,990 for a 4-month programme but delivered only 1 month’s medicine and keeps lying about it." (16 Oct 2026) [D3-04-F40] | "It's been almost 20 days i have cancelled my order and i have not been refunded my money..." (BeatO, 12 Jul 2026) [D3-04-F42] |
| Praise for a named coach | "The support from my coach was effective and without her knowledge and support throughout the program I could not have achieved my goal." (Fitterfly, 23 Apr 2025) [D3-04-F43] | "Now my HBA1c reduced to 6.1 and medicine also reduced to half." (Fitterfly, 10 Nov 2024) [D3-04-F44] |

None of the 300 reviews mentions language or voice, and none describes a dose change from a home reading (count from the research note's method section).

#### Reminders and messages

In a Punjab trial at two public hospitals, 388 patients with uncontrolled pressure got two myth-busting WhatsApp reminders before their visit or none; attendance was 21.8% against 19.6%, a null result, and beliefs did not change [D3-04-F50]. A Delhi study of 110 patients (counselling, voice calls, SMS) reported control rising from 14.7% to 52.9%, with no control group [D3-04-F51]. Who holds the phone that receives such messages is in A12.

#### Two field voices from people who run programmes

Both are LinkedIn posts, paraphrased; numbers inside them are unverified.

- A national NCD (non-communicable disease) consultant at UNICEF India, about Apr 2026: programmes failed on BP machines uncalibrated for months and mid-month drug stock-outs; one protocol, steady supply and the Simple app made missed visits visible. Claims control rose 48 percentage points in primary care and 23 in secondary (POST CLAIM, source not named) (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026).
- A doctor and WHO consultant, about Oct 2026: counting visits is not enough; programmes must know who continues, who is controlled and who missed follow-up. Cites mWellcare (Appendix B14): a digital system does not guarantee results (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026).

Neither describes dose changes from home readings.

### A14. What we could not find

- **Specialists and doctors:** current counts of endocrinologists, cardiologists, nephrologists, chest physicians and physiotherapists; doctors per 1,000 people, rural against urban.
- **Disease counts:** a heart-failure count newer than 2016; dose levels in any Indian heart-failure registry [D1-01-F35]; a stroke-survivor count from a primary source; depression prevalence after 2015-16 from a primary source; a depression-only treatment gap.
- **Follow-up:** the share of chronic patients who see a doctor each year; loss to follow-up outside IHCI; HbA1c at insulin start in India; how long a dose change is delayed, in months.
- **Cost:** household cost per chronic-care visit; travel distance and lost wages.
- **Phones:** official WhatsApp India users; unique smartphone users from a regulator.
- **Japan and the world:** Japan's 2023-24 hypertension control rate; a dated WHO India NCD death share.
- **Voices:** a household figure for cuff ownership; any Indian doctor, nurse or health worker on dose steps from home readings; any qualitative study of ASHAs on blood-pressure follow-up; any patient voice on a dose increase; voice against text preference among older patients; Reddit posts (the archive timed out) and Google Play reviews.

### A15. Terms used in this document

- **Adaptive depth:** 0-4 score for how far a product changes treatment (A2).
- **Adherence:** taking the medicine as prescribed.
- **ANM:** auxiliary nurse midwife.
- **ASHA:** a village health worker.
- **AYUSH:** practitioners of traditional medicine.
- **Basal insulin:** long-acting insulin.
- **Biofeedback:** a body signal shown back to the patient.
- **Care cascade:** following people with a condition through four steps: has it, knows it, is treated, is controlled.
- **CGM:** continuous glucose monitor, a glucose sensor worn on the body.
- **CHC:** community health centre.
- **CHO:** community health officer.
- **Closed loop:** a device that measures and adjusts therapy itself.
- **COPD:** chronic lung disease.
- **Denominator:** the group a percentage is taken of.
- **Digital therapeutic:** software that changes one patient's treatment.
- **DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis):** a dangerous acid build-up.
- **Endpoint:** the result a trial is judged on.
- **Fixed-dose combination:** two drugs in one tablet.
- **Hazard ratio:** a risk ratio measured over time; below 1 means fewer events.
- **HbA1c:** blood test of average sugar over about three months.
- **Heart-failure guideline drug classes:** beta blocker, RAS blocker (ACE inhibitor or ARB) and MRA.
- **HWC:** health and wellness centre.
- **IHCI:** India Hypertension Control Initiative, a government programme with a fixed drug protocol.
- **INR:** clotting test that sets the warfarin dose.
- **Insulin inertia:** delay in starting or raising insulin.
- **Masked uncontrolled pressure:** high at home, normal in clinic.
- **NCD:** non-communicable disease.
- **Not significant:** small enough to be chance (a null result).
- **NT-proBNP:** a blood marker of heart strain.
- **Protocol:** a written step-by-step treatment plan.
- **Randomised trial:** people get treatments by chance.
- **Risk ratio:** risk with treatment divided by risk without; below 1 means lower risk.
- **SMART:** one inhaler for both maintenance and relief, so each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose.
- **Systolic:** the upper blood-pressure number, in mmHg (millimetres of mercury).
- **Time in range:** share of the day with sugar at 70-180 mg/dL.
- **Titration:** stepping a dose towards a target.

### A16. So what for us

OUR VIEW.
- **The fund asks for a routine treatment decision between visits,** from a home reading, by someone the patient can reach. Level 4 on the adaptive depth scale is the entry condition, however good the sensor (A2).
- **Blood pressure first.** On any count it is the largest pool: 35.5% of adults 20+, against 11.4% for diabetes on the same survey [D1-03-F01].
- **The leak is after treatment starts.** Two steps of the cascade leak, diagnosis and control. Over 95% of diagnosed Tamil Nadu patients are treated, yet the hypertension control rate was 35.4% (denominator not stated) [D1-03-F09]. The step from "treated" to "controlled" depends on the dose being raised and the medicine being taken, which is the decision our loop prepares.
- **Screening and enrolment are already huge** and run at crore scale [D1-03-F20]; the missing piece is the dose change between visits. A loop that feeds the existing protocol and records fits the system rather than competing with it.
- **The return visit is the bottleneck.** 51% of IHCI patients returned, and among those who returned control rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10]. Our loop must reach the half who do not come back, between visits. For blood pressure, the pilot should measure the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned.
- **The scarce thing is the prescriber's decision,** which waits for a visit that about half the patients do not make. About 80% of required rural CHC posts in four specialities (surgeon, physician, obstetrician-gynaecologist, paediatrician) were unfilled in March 2023 [D1-03-F16], and visits lasted about two minutes in 2013-2015 [D1-03-F24]. A two-minute visit has no time to read two weeks of home readings. Software should prepare the next protocol step for a general doctor or nurse to approve, with the specialist owning the protocol.
- **Patient costs.** Avoided trips save patients money, but without a rupee figure per visit we cannot yet claim a saving.
- **Not only an Indian product.** Treated but not controlled is the gap in Japan too.
- **Heart failure.** A clear dose gap with high death rates, but safe titration needs lab values, so heart failure is a later protocol for the same engine.
- **Assume most patients do not own a cuff.** Only 18.1% used one even among clinic attenders [D3-04-F06]. The loop must bring the cuff, the teaching and the thresholds.
- **Feeling well** recurs as a reason to stop, and a home reading is one thing that can contradict it.
- **A doctor's approval cannot be assumed.** A doctor may not trust the state protocol, so each proposal must show why the step is safe, answering the fears of slow control and side effects [D3-04-F15].
- **Never rely on a reminder alone.** WhatsApp reminders did not raise attendance [D3-04-F50]. A message only works if it reaches the person who holds the phone and leads to a decision.
- **Design for the household phone.** 57.4% of rural women own a phone [D1-03-F42], so about four in ten do not (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 57.4 = 42.6%). The design must work on a shared phone, through a health worker, and by voice, in the local language [D3-04-F05, D3-04-F23].
- **Risk: home readings bring bad news.** 21.8% of treated clinic attenders had masked uncontrolled pressure [D3-04-F09]; expect fear of more drugs and the urge to stop [D3-04-F02].
