## Appendix A. The challenge, the burden and the voices in detail

This appendix holds the detail behind chapter 1: what the fund's challenge asks a product to do (A1 to A3), how many people in India it concerns and how few are controlled (A4 to A8), why care breaks down between visits (A9 to A12), and what patients and doctors say in public (A13). The trials behind the challenge's demands are in Appendix B.

### A1. The challenge, phrase by phrase

This section turns each phrase of the fund's challenge into what a product must do. The middle column is our reading of each phrase. Terms are explained in A15.

| The fund's words | What a product must do (OUR VIEW) | Facts behind it |
|---|---|---|
| "rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers" | A signal that moves within days of a treatment change and is cheap and correct to measure at home. | Bluetooth cuff: about ₹2,500-2,900 (online listings, mid-2026 or undated; search summary only) [D1-06-F31]. Signal speeds: Appendix B3. |
| "continuously personalise care" | Recompute the treatment from this patient's readings: protocol step, response to the last step, medicine taken or not, what is unsafe. | Gujarat's hypertension sheet: "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" [D1-06-F14]. |
| "adaptive to patient needs between appointments" | Change the treatment without waiting for the next visit. | 51% of 21,895 patients at 24 government hypertension programme sites returned for follow-up (A6) [D1-03-F10]. |
| "measurable improvements in health outcomes" | One endpoint that can move in 90 days, with an accepted threshold for "clinically meaningful" (A3). | An independent US review (October 2024) set it at 5 mmHg of systolic pressure (the upper number) [D1-01-F39]. |
| "patients who cannot access frequent specialist support" | Move the routine decision to a general doctor, nurse or health worker under a written protocol. The specialist owns the protocol and sees the exceptions. | 79.9% of required specialist posts at rural community health centres were unfilled (A9) [D1-03-F16]. |
| "beyond monitoring and reminders" | Reach adaptive depth 4: the therapy itself changes (A2). | Self-monitoring alone: 1.0 mmHg; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or lifestyle counselling): 6.1 (Appendix B4) [D1-01-F05]. |

### A2. What "beyond monitoring and reminders" rules in and out

This document scores every product on an "adaptive depth" scale from 0 to 4. The fund names levels 1 and 2. OUR VIEW: it is asking for level 4.

| Level | Examples in the notes | What the evidence shows |
|---|---|---|
| 0: uses no patient data | Nerivio migraine wearable, switched on by the patient, rated 0-1 [D1-02-F12]. India: none rated 0 | Nothing adapts. |
| 1: shows data | India: pocket ECGs (search summary only) [D1-04-F32]. Abroad: Omron VitalSight [D1-01-F39] | Self-monitoring alone: no effect [D1-01-F05]; one exception, a glucose sensor (Appendix B5) [D1-01-F42]. |
| 2: reminders, generic content | India: government Simple app, with overdue lists and reminder messages [D3-05-F03]. Abroad: Medisafe reminder app | Medisafe reminder app against control: 0.5 mmHg, not significant (Appendix B9) [D1-01-F06]. |
| 3: coaching from the person's own data | India: Sugar.fit, BeatO, Fitterfly [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. Abroad: CureApp HT, Japan | CureApp HT against lifestyle advice alone: 24-hour systolic 2.4 mmHg lower (Appendix B4) [D1-01-F07]. |
| 4: changes the therapy (dose, protocol step, exercise prescription) | India: only Sanofi's My Dose Coach found, its Indian results unconfirmed [D1-04-F09]. Abroad: d-Nav; insulin pumps [D1-05-F41] | d-Nav dose device against clinician support alone: HbA1c (three-month average sugar) down 1.0 point against 0.3 (Appendix B5) [D1-01-F13]. |

**The line between 3 and 4.** Level 3 changes the advice: what to eat, how to exercise. Level 4 changes the prescription: a new dose or protocol step. A clinician approving each change keeps it at level 4. Indian diabetes programmes sit at 3: no page says sensor data changes a drug dose [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. The test: after the software runs, the prescription is different.

The loop that level 4 needs (sense, decide, confirm, act, learn) is set out in Appendix B1 (picture in chapter 1).

### A3. What "measurable" means

One endpoint per condition that a pilot could read at about 90 days. The trials behind each effect are described in full in Appendix B.

| Condition | Endpoint | Effect the trials found | "Clinically meaningful" threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| High blood pressure | Share under 140/90 [D1-06-F03] | 57.2% controlled with pharmacist dose changes from home readings, against 30.0% with usual care (Appendix B4) [D1-01-F04] | 5 mmHg systolic against usual care [D1-01-F39] |
| Type 2 diabetes on insulin | HbA1c | Down 1.44-1.48 points with daily dose proposals, against 0.92 with standard care (Appendix B5) [D1-01-F14] | None given; a US review judged 0.23-0.60 points not meaningful for type 2 tools without a continuous sensor [D1-05-F04] |
| Diabetes with a sensor | Time in range | Up 14 points with a dose algorithm (Appendix B5) [D1-01-F43] | NOT RESEARCHED |
| Heart failure | Readmission or death | 15.2% against 23.3% at 180 days with fast dose stepping after discharge, adjusted estimates (Appendix B6) [D1-01-F27] | NOT RESEARCHED |
| Warfarin | Time in the target INR range | Trials against usual care report clots (risk ratio 0.47) and deaths (0.55) instead (Appendix B7) [D1-02-F05] | NOT RESEARCHED |

No blood-pressure dose-change trial in our first-round notes reported before 6 months [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F04].

### A4. How many people

The surveys measure different ages, use different blood-pressure rules and ran in different years, so they disagree. We give each figure with its source and do not pick one.

| Condition | Figure | Year of data | Who was counted | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High blood pressure | 35.5% | 2008-2020 | ICMR-INDIAB, adults 20+, measured BP, 113,043 people, 31 states and union territories | [D1-03-F01] |
| High blood pressure | 315 million people, a 2021 projection by the survey's investigators, not a count in the paper | 2008-2020 survey, projected to 2021 | Same study, investigators' commentary and press | [D1-03-F02] |
| High blood pressure | 22.6%; 24% of men, 21% of women (search summary only) | 2019-21 | NFHS-5 (National Family Health Survey), ages 15+ | [D1-03-F03, D1-03-F04] |
| High blood pressure | 45.9% | 2017-19 | LASI (Longitudinal Ageing Study in India), adults 45+, 72,262 people | [D1-03-F25] |
| High blood pressure | 22.1% of men, 19.4% of women, elevated or on drugs (search summary only, provisional) | 2023-24 | NFHS-6 | [D1-03-F22] |
| Diabetes | 11.4%; prediabetes 15.3% | 2008-2020 | ICMR-INDIAB, adults 20+ | [D1-03-F01] |
| Diabetes | 101 million; prediabetes 136 million, 2021 projections by the survey's investigators, not counts in the paper | 2008-2020 survey, projected to 2021 | Same study, investigators' commentary and press | [D1-03-F02] |
| Diabetes | 89.8 million (age-standardised 10.5%); 156.7 million projected for 2050 | 2024 | IDF Diabetes Atlas, adults 20-79 | [D1-03-F28] |
| Diabetes | 20.9% of men, 17.8% of women with high sugar or on drugs, against 15.6% and 13.5% in NFHS-5 (search summary only, provisional) | 2023-24 | NFHS-6, random glucose (a screening test) | [D1-03-F22] |
| COPD (chronic lung disease); asthma | 55.3 million; 37.9 million (search summary only) | 2016 | GBD state study | [D1-03-F36] |
| Chronic kidney disease | 13.24% pooled; an older review 3-4% by a different method (search summary only) | 2011-2023 | Community studies | [D1-03-F37] |
| Heart failure | 1.3-4.6 million cases, or about 8-10 million; the estimates differ (see A7) | 2010; 2016 | Reviews built from local and disease-specific data, no national survey | [D3-07-F24, D3-07-F25] |

Why they differ, as the notes give it:
- **Blood pressure, 35.5% against 22.6%.** Different ages (20+ against 15+), years and use of the BP threshold [D1-03-F01, D1-03-F04]. LASI counts only people 45+ [D1-03-F25].
- **Diabetes, 101 million against 89.8 million.** Different survey base and age definition; the 101 million is a 2021 projection of survey rates [D1-03-F02, D1-03-F28].
- **NFHS-6.** Random glucose is a screening test, and the findings are provisional [D1-03-F22].

### A5. The care cascade

(Picture in chapter 1: the share of adults with high blood pressure who know, are treated and are controlled, 2018-19 and 2023-24.)

A care cascade follows people with a condition through four steps: has it, knows it, is treated, is controlled. Percentages compare only when the denominator (the group the percentage is taken of) is the same, and several sources do not state it clearly.

#### High blood pressure

| Source | Aware or diagnosed | Treated | Controlled | Denominator | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NFHS-5 district paper, 2019-21 [D1-03-F05] | 46.0% (district average; range 6.1-89.6%) | 18.7% | Not used: the abstract gives 32.9% "of individuals with hypertension", which cannot sit above 18.7% treated; the preprint below gives 9.1% of all for the same 2019-21 survey [D1-03-F07] | Contested; do not read this row as one chain | Abstract opened |
| NFHS-5 preprint, 1.69 million adults, 2019-21 [D1-03-F07] | 36.7% (about 1 in 3) | 17.7% (under 1 in 5) | 9.1% (about 1 in 11) | All people with hypertension | Preprint; record opened |
| NFHS-5 and NFHS-4, ages 15-49 (Cureus 2023) [D1-03-F06] | | | 73.7% (80.8% in NFHS-4) | Only people on BP drugs, ages 15-49 | Abstract opened |
| LASI, adults 45+, 2017-19 [D1-03-F25] | 55.7% | 38.9% | 31.7% | All hypertensives for the first two; **control denominator not stated, check before use** | Abstract opened |
| LASI, self-reported [D1-03-F26] | 4 in 10 not aware | 73% of the aware | 10% of the treated | Changes at each step | Search summary only |

The same survey gives 73.7% controlled when only people aged 15-49 on drugs are counted, and 9.1% (about 1 in 11) when everyone with hypertension is counted; the ages and denominators differ, so the two do not compare [D1-03-F06, D1-03-F07]. A LASI preprint found 63.8% of measured hypertension undiagnosed, about 46 million older Indians (search summary only) [D1-03-F27].

**The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) district surveys.** The government programme surveyed the same 9 districts in 5 states twice. The surveys are before and after, with no comparison districts [D1-01-F10, D1-01-F11, D1-03-F12]. The 2018-19 source was opened.

| | 2018-19 | 2023-24 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| People with hypertension | 7,047 [D1-01-F10] | 7,324 [D1-01-F11] | |
| Aware | 52.4% [D1-01-F10] | 58.5% [D1-03-F12] | +6.1 points (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
| Treated | 40.8% [D1-01-F10] | 44.7% [D1-03-F12] | +3.9 points (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
| Controlled | 14.5% [D1-01-F10] | 21.2% [D1-01-F11] | +6.7 points [D1-03-F12] |

In 2018-19, control was under 5% in two of the districts [D1-01-F10].

#### Diabetes

- **Undiagnosed:** 43%, about 38.6 million, in 2024 [D1-03-F28].
- **Treated but not controlled:** in Tamil Nadu over 95% of diagnosed people were treated, yet the diabetes control rate was 9.8% (the abstract does not state the denominator; survey detail in A6) [D1-03-F09].
- **Slow insulin starts:** a mean of 7 years of diabetes before insulin in one older Indian study (search summary only) [D1-03-F30]. AIIMS Bhopal clinic records (950 patients, not a trial) classed 11.8% as insulin inertia (delay in starting or raising insulin), mean HbA1c (a blood test showing average sugar over about three months) 8.43% [D1-03-F29].

### A6. Treatment is not control, and half do not return

Two Indian data sets show that getting people onto medicine is not enough, and that people who return do far better than those who do not.

**Tamil Nadu survey.** The state's doorstep programme, Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam, was surveyed in 6,856 adults aged 30+ across all 38 districts (paper abstract, 2025; a South First news report gives 6,809) [D1-03-F09]. Screening reached 79.4% for diabetes and 82.6% for hypertension, and over 95% of diagnosed people were on treatment. Control rates remained low: 9.8% for diabetes and 35.4% for hypertension; the abstract does not say whether these are shares of everyone with the disease, the diagnosed or the treated [D1-03-F09]. How the scheme delivers medicines is in Appendix B13.

**IHCI cohort.** A government programme with a fixed drug protocol. The cohort registered 21,895 patients at 24 sentinel sites in Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Telangana (Jan 2018-Jun 2019), followed up Jul-Sep 2019, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10].
- Only 11,274 (51%) returned [D1-03-F10].
- Among returners, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% [D1-03-F10].
- Control was 70.4% in primary care against 52.2% in secondary care [D1-03-F10].
- Protocol drugs: amlodipine, telmisartan or losartan, chlorthalidone or hydrochlorothiazide; 44.6% were on amlodipine 5 mg alone at follow-up [D1-03-F11].

A second IHCI cohort, in Punjab and Maharashtra, gives a different loss figure; the two are compared in Appendix B11.

**Return visits.** About 27% of registered IHCI patients did not return in Jan-Mar 2021 (search summary only) [D1-03-F13]. IHCI enrolled about 4 million patients, about 12.5% of the estimated total, by around 2022 (search summary only) [D1-03-F13]. Pooled Indian non-adherence to BP drugs is 48%, with a prediction interval of 9-90% (search summary only) [D1-03-F44]. The reasons patients give for missing visits are in A13.

### A7. Heart failure and stroke in India

No national count of heart failure was found, and the estimates differ widely: 1.3 to 4.6 million cases in a 2010 estimate built from disease-specific figures, whose authors say no surveillance exists (quoted in a 2024 review) [D3-07-F24], against about 8 to 10 million, about 1% of the population, in a 2016 review of local and global studies (search summary only) [D3-07-F25]. For stroke, the Global Burden of Disease study put India's prevalent cases at 9.4 million in 2021, up from 4.4 million in 1990, with over 1.25 million new cases a year (press report quoting the authors) [D3-07-F26].

The registries show patients leave hospital on too few of the drugs that work and stop them afterwards. The three guideline classes are beta blocker, RAS blocker (ACE inhibitor or ARB) and MRA.

| Registry | Who | Treatment finding | Outcome | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Heart Failure Registry | 10,851 acute patients, 53 hospitals, 21 states | 47.5% of eligible patients on guideline drugs | 90-day mortality 14.2%; 1-year mortality 22.1% | [D1-01-F47, D1-01-F48] |
| Indian College of Cardiology registry | 5,182 acute patients, 17 centres, 2019-2021 | All three classes taken: 18.8% of men, 15.9% of women | 1-year death 18.1% | [D1-01-F49] |
| Trivandrum, Kerala | 1,205 admissions, 16 hospitals, 2013 | Only 25% of patients with weak pumping discharged on all three drug classes | 5-year mortality 59% | [D1-01-F35] |
| NORIN-STEMI, Delhi | Heart-attack patients with weak pumping | Use of one class (MRA) fell from 69% at discharge to 6% at 1 year | | [D1-01-F50] |

The national registries differ (47.5% against about 17%) partly because one counts prescription and the other adherence [D1-01-F49]. The registries report drug classes, not dose levels; none reports doses as a share of target [D1-01-F35, D1-01-F47, D1-01-F49]. The trials of dose stepping and telemonitoring in heart failure are in Appendix B6.

### A8. The world and Japan

Low control is a world problem, and Japan, the fund's home, has a large, old population with high blood pressure.

| Measure | Figure | Year | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| World hypertension (30-79) | About 1.4 billion; 44% unaware; 23% controlled; two-thirds in low- and middle-income countries | 2024 | [D1-03-F32] |
| World diabetes | 830 million adults; 59% of those 30+ not on diabetes medicine | 2022 | [D1-03-F33] |
| Japan hypertension | About 43 million; about 31 million (73%) poorly controlled (search summary only) | 2010 base, cited for 2017 | [D1-03-F47] |
| Japan aged 65+ | 29.4% (Sep 2025); 34.8% projected for 2040 (search summary only) | 2025 | [D1-03-F48] |
| Japan visit length | 10.2 minutes | 2012 | [D1-03-F24] |

### A9. The specialist and time gap

Few specialists work where most patients live, and doctors who see chronic patients have very little time per visit. This is what the challenge's phrase "patients who cannot access frequent specialist support" means in India.

**Rural community health centre (CHC) specialist posts, March 2023** [D1-03-F16]:

| Specialty | Shortfall | Share of required posts |
|---|---|---|
| Surgeon | 4,578 | 83.3% [D1-03-F16] |
| Physician | 4,499 | 81.9% [D1-03-F16] |
| Paediatrician | 4,425 | 80.5% [D1-03-F16] |
| Obstetrician-gynaecologist | 4,078 | 74.2% [D1-03-F16] |
| All four | 17,551 of 21,964 (4,413 in post) | 79.9% [D1-03-F16] |

The article's rows sum to 17,580, not 17,551 [D1-03-F16]. The shortfall has stayed near 17,500 since 2014-15 [D1-03-F17].

**Specialist counts.** The only figures are from a 2017 parliamentary committee (search summary only): about 4,000 cardiologists, 1,200 nephrologists and 650 endocrinologists, against the committee's estimated needs of 88,000, 40,000 and 28,000 [D1-03-F18]. The government told Parliament it does not hold speciality-wise doctor data (news report of the reply, 13 Apr 2025) [D3-07-F22].

**Consultation length.** Indian primary-care visits lasted about 2.3 minutes (2013, stopwatch, 412 visits) and 2 minutes (2015) [D1-03-F24]. Japan's, for comparison, lasted 10.2 minutes in 2012 (A8) [D1-03-F24].

**Doctor ratio and its caveat.** The government gave 1:811 in Rajya Sabha (about 2 Dec 2025), counting 13,88,185 allopathic doctors plus 7,51,768 AYUSH practitioners (traditional medicine) and "assuming that 80 per cent" are available [D1-03-F40]. Allopathic doctors alone give a lower ratio. OUR ARITHMETIC from the note: 13,88,185 x 0.8 = about 11.1 lakh, about 0.79 per 1,000 people if the population is about 1.4 billion (an assumption, not sourced) [D1-03-F40].

### A10. Cost and follow-up

Families pay a large share of health costs themselves, and the share rose in the latest year on record.

- **Out-of-pocket share:** 39.4% of total health expenditure in 2021-22 and 43.41% in 2022-23 (National Health Accounts released 27 May 2026, via a news report) [D1-03-F23]. In 2022-23 household spending rose by ₹26,375 crore while government spending fell by nearly ₹49,000 crore [D1-03-F23].
- **Per visit:** medicines were 61.15% of spend per outpatient spell in a Delhi report; another report says median outpatient spend is zero (search summary only) [D1-03-F49].
- **Cheaper medicines:** 18,646 Jan Aushadhi Kendras (generic medicine shops), Feb 2026, priced 50-80% below branded [D1-03-F20].
- **Diabetes spend:** about US$109.5 per person and over US$9.8 billion in total (IDF 2024) [D1-03-F28].

The cost of a chronic-care visit to the household, and how long a dose change is delayed, were not found (A14).

### A11. Public programmes and their scale

India already screens and treats at large scale through free public programmes, the channels a loop would plug into.

| Programme | Scale (date) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| National NCD screening drives | 41.5 crore screened for hypertension, 41.3 crore for diabetes (cumulative, Aug 2026) | [D1-03-F20] |
| Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (12 free services) | Over 1.86 lakh functional (Aug 2026) | [D1-03-F19] |
| NCD clinics | 770 district clinics; 6,410 at CHCs (2026) | [D1-03-F20] |
| Tamil Nadu doorstep care | Two crore beneficiaries by Dec 2024 (search summary only) | [D1-03-F46] |
| eSanjeevani teleconsultation | Over 49 crore consultations by Aug 2026; 2.4 lakh providers | [D1-03-F19] |
| ABHA digital health ID | 96.43 crore IDs; over 110 crore records linked (Aug 2026) | [D1-03-F19] |

Progress against the "75 by 25" target (75 million on standard care by 2025) is in Appendix E [D1-03-F14]. How IHCI and Tamil Nadu's scheme run in practice is in Appendix B11 and B13.

### A12. Phones and who is left out

Most Indians have a mobile connection, but rural women and older people are least likely to own a phone, and the phone is often not the patient's.

| Measure | Figure | Year | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Smartphone owners | Over 622 million (industry estimate) | 2025 | [D1-03-F41] |
| Internet users | Over 915 million, 48% women (industry estimate) | 2025 | [D1-03-F41] |
| Internet subscriptions | 1.09 billion connections, not unique people (search summary only) | Mar 2026 | [D1-03-F31] |
| Women 15-49 owning a phone | 63.6%; rural 57.4% (search summary only) | 2023-24 | [D1-03-F42] |
| Women 15-49 who own the phone they use | 54%; rural 46.6% | Not stated | [D3-04-F23] |
| Phone ownership, 15+ | Men 83.9%, women 56.2% (search summary only) | 2025 | [D1-03-F42] |
| Rural older adults near Mysore, 150 people | 50% owned a phone, few a smartphone; digital literacy 11% | Not stated | [D3-04-F56] |
| eSanjeevani users | Women 57.14%; age 60+ 16.25% (search summary only) | 2026 | [D1-03-F21] |
| Indians who spoke English | About 10.6% | 2011 | [D3-04-F57] |

The two figures for women aged 15-49 differ (63.6% owning a phone, 54% owning the phone they use); our source parts give no year for the second and no reason for the gap [D1-03-F42, D3-04-F23].

**The phone is often not the patient's.** Caregivers enable access for older adults and devices are shared (A13) [D3-04-F05]; one review moves a meter from a husband's phone to a mother's [D3-04-F25].

### A13. What patients and doctors say in public

The team has done no interviews, so this section stands in until it does. It reports published interview studies, surveys, public app reviews and posts, labelled PUBLISHED STUDY, PUBLIC REVIEW or FORUM POST. None of it is customer evidence gathered by the team; reviews are self-selected and studies were read as abstracts only.

#### Why patients miss follow-up and stop medicines

Eight Indian interview studies (PUBLISHED STUDY) name the same causes: feeling well, cost, family duties, fear of long-term drugs, traditional medicine.

| Where | People | Barriers, in the authors' words |
|---|---|---|
| Coastal Karnataka, tertiary hospital | 32 hypertensive patients lost to follow-up | "symptom-driven healthcare seeking, medication non-adherence, occupational responsibilities, and competing family priorities"; wage loss, rushed consultations [D3-04-F01] |
| Rural Tamil Nadu (Thiruvallur) | 15 adults with diabetes or hypertension | Stopping is structural, unintentional (work, travel, caregiving) or intentional, "perceived harm, symptoms or treatment need"; "Family relationships could both support and hinder medication-taking" [D3-04-F02] |
| Tehri, Uttarakhand | 40 (20 diabetes, 20 hypertension) | "the use of alternative medicine"; "lack of self-management guidance from their physicians" [D3-04-F03] |
| West Garo Hills, Meghalaya | 52 (providers, health workers, community) | "concern about long-term treatment"; "a preference for traditional medicine constrained screening efforts"; elders decide [D3-04-F12, D3-04-F48] |
| Rural Meghalaya | 29 women aged 60+ with diabetes | "caregiving roles as barriers to care"; "feelings of guilt due to financial dependency" [D3-04-F04] |
| Rural Punjab | 8 focus groups plus 15 health professionals | "beliefs in alternative therapies, drug side effects"; "Physicians' guidance and support were motivating them" [D3-04-F13] |
| Ludhiana, urban health centre | 40 with diabetes | "side effects of taking medications daily"; "about 50% patients were adherent" [D3-04-F14] |
| Chennai and Chunampet | 54 (patients, caregivers, providers, officials) | Caregivers enable access for older adults; "shared device ownership"; "data privacy, security, and app reliability affected trust" [D3-04-F05] |

Karnataka patients suggested reminders and digital records [D3-04-F01]. A FORUM POST by an adult child says the father's pressure stayed controlled on Ayurvedic treatment, then rose, and he "re-started some medication" [D3-04-F52].

The same reasons appear in numbers in one IHCI district. A Bathinda (Punjab) phone survey of 157 people who had missed visits for over 3 months, a small convenience sample, found: no sense of being ill 24.8%, distance 22.2%, no guidance or reminder 15.2%, acute illness 8.2% [D3-05-F07].

#### Home monitors in Indian homes

Few patients own a home cuff, most taught themselves, and home readings show that many "controlled" patients are not.

- **Who has one.** Of 2,588 clinic-attending people with hypertension and caregivers in North India, 18.1% used a home monitor (urban 20.5%, rural 8.5%) [D3-04-F06]. No household figure exists; a web claim of under 5% cites no source [D3-04-F22].
- **Who taught them.** 75.2% reported "learning HBPM themselves through observation, videos, and reading"; 24.7% were trained by a health worker. Technique was excellent in 15.9% of patients and 5.9% of caregivers [D3-04-F06].
- **Do doctors act on home readings.** About 88% of 832 Indian doctors recommend home monitoring, but estimate only 30.4% of patients measure; 31.3% say to measure before tablets, about 30% give no instructions [D3-04-F07]. Only 15.1% knew the correct home thresholds [D3-04-F18].
- **What home readings reveal.** In GRAND (18 centres, 12 states, 1,920 treated regular attenders, 7 days of home readings), 77.7% looked controlled by clinic pressure but 55.9% by clinic plus home; 21.8% had masked uncontrolled pressure (high at home, normal in clinic) [D3-04-F09]. Median knowledge of home monitoring was 1 out of 7 [D3-04-F10].

#### What doctors and health workers say

Doctors describe heavy workloads, and many private doctors do not follow the state protocol.

- **Workload.** In Kolar, Karnataka: "Doctors face very high workloads, especially in the public sector"; care is "very doctor-centred" [D3-04-F16]. Meghalaya reports staff vacancies and limited training [D3-04-F12, D3-04-F20].
- **The state protocol.** Of 30 private doctors in Bhopal, 19 did not follow it, citing "fear of either losing patients due to a lack of immediate blood pressure control or causing drug-related adverse effects" and a preference for fixed-dose combinations (two drugs in one tablet) [D3-04-F15].
- **Health workers with a decision tool.** IMPACT Diabetes, a cluster trial in 16 villages in two states (418 people, 9 months): ASHAs (village health workers) with a tablet tool under physician supervision, against usual care. HbA1c fell by 0.5 or more in 21.8% against 10.3%; physician visits 85.0% against 29.8%; "acceptable and feasible for patients, ASHAs, and physicians" [D3-04-F17]. Diabetes, not blood pressure.

No Indian doctor, nurse or health worker was found speaking about dose steps from home readings (A14).

#### What users say about existing programmes

The latest 100 Apple App Store India reviews each of three diabetes programmes, BeatO, Sugar.fit and Fitterfly, were read on 13 Nov 2026. One-star reviews: 55, 76 and 9 (count from the research note's method section); Fitterfly's 5-star profile looks prompted (the note's inference). All quotes are PUBLIC REVIEW, verbatim.

| Theme | Quote 1 | Quote 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Spam calls | "Please stop calling and sending WhatsApp messages about webinar. I never signed up for it." (Sugar.fit, 17 Oct 2026) [D3-04-F27] | "we will get continuous pre recorded calls to join sugarfit class everyday atleast 5 calls." (Sugar.fit, 26 Jul 2026) [D3-04-F28] |
| No reachable person | "Since 5 days I am trying for doctor appointment but no slot available" (Sugar.fit, 21 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F30] | "Unable to access blood reports and unable to reach any support or helpline number." (Sugar.fit, 12 Oct 2026) [D3-04-F29] |
| Coaching runs dry | "by the third month, there is hardly anything new to discuss." (Sugar.fit, 26 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F33] | "no results no calling or follow ups aftee 1 month" (Sugar.fit, 25 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F34] |
| Device and data | "sensor got activated, but data never synced." (BeatO, 2 Sep 2026) [D3-04-F36] | "Within five minutes, I got five readings with a difference of over 50." (BeatO, 17 Mar 2026) [D3-04-F37] |
| Money and medicine | "Sugar.fit took ₹18,990 for a 4-month programme but delivered only 1 month’s medicine and keeps lying about it." (16 Oct 2026) [D3-04-F40] | "It's been almost 20 days i have cancelled my order and i have not been refunded my money..." (BeatO, 12 Jul 2026) [D3-04-F42] |
| Praise for a named coach | "The support from my coach was effective and without her knowledge and support throughout the program I could not have achieved my goal." (Fitterfly, 23 Apr 2025) [D3-04-F43] | "Now my HBA1c reduced to 6.1 and medicine also reduced to half." (Fitterfly, 10 Nov 2024) [D3-04-F44] |

None of the 300 reviews mentions language or voice, and none describes a dose change from a home reading (count from the research note's method section).

#### Reminders and messages

In a Punjab trial at two public hospitals, 388 patients with uncontrolled pressure got two myth-busting WhatsApp reminders before their visit or none; attendance was 21.8% against 19.6%, a null result, and beliefs did not change [D3-04-F50]. A Delhi study of 110 patients (counselling, voice calls, SMS) reported control rising from 14.7% to 52.9%, with no control group [D3-04-F51]. Who holds the phone that receives such messages is in A12.

#### Two field voices from people who run programmes

Both are LinkedIn posts, paraphrased; numbers inside them are unverified.

- A national NCD (non-communicable disease) consultant at UNICEF India, about Apr 2026: programmes failed on BP machines uncalibrated for months and mid-month drug stock-outs; one protocol, steady supply and the Simple app made missed visits visible. Claims control rose 48 percentage points in primary care and 23 in secondary (POST CLAIM, source not named) (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026).
- A doctor and WHO consultant, about Oct 2026: counting visits is not enough; programmes must know who continues, who is controlled and who missed follow-up. Cites mWellcare (Appendix B14): a digital system does not guarantee results (LinkedIn, read 13 Nov 2026).

Neither describes dose changes from home readings.

### A14. What we could not find

- **Specialists and doctors:** current counts of endocrinologists, cardiologists, nephrologists, chest physicians and physiotherapists; doctors per 1,000 people, rural against urban.
- **Disease counts:** a heart-failure count newer than 2016; dose levels in any Indian heart-failure registry [D1-01-F35]; a stroke-survivor count from a primary source; depression prevalence after 2015-16 from a primary source; a depression-only treatment gap.
- **Follow-up:** the share of chronic patients who see a doctor each year; loss to follow-up outside IHCI; HbA1c at insulin start in India; how long a dose change is delayed, in months.
- **Cost:** household cost per chronic-care visit; travel distance and lost wages.
- **Phones:** official WhatsApp India users; unique smartphone users from a regulator.
- **Japan and the world:** Japan's 2023-24 hypertension control rate; a dated WHO India NCD death share.
- **Voices:** a household figure for cuff ownership; any Indian doctor, nurse or health worker on dose steps from home readings; any qualitative study of ASHAs on blood-pressure follow-up; any patient voice on a dose increase; voice against text preference among older patients; Reddit posts (the archive timed out) and Google Play reviews.

### A15. Terms used in this document

- **Adaptive depth:** 0-4 score for how far a product changes treatment (A2).
- **Adherence:** taking the medicine as prescribed.
- **ANM:** auxiliary nurse midwife.
- **ASHA:** a village health worker.
- **AYUSH:** practitioners of traditional medicine.
- **Basal insulin:** long-acting insulin.
- **Biofeedback:** a body signal shown back to the patient.
- **Care cascade:** following people with a condition through four steps: has it, knows it, is treated, is controlled.
- **CGM:** continuous glucose monitor, a glucose sensor worn on the body.
- **CHC:** community health centre.
- **CHO:** community health officer.
- **Closed loop:** a device that measures and adjusts therapy itself.
- **COPD:** chronic lung disease.
- **Denominator:** the group a percentage is taken of.
- **Digital therapeutic:** software that changes one patient's treatment.
- **DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis):** a dangerous acid build-up.
- **Endpoint:** the result a trial is judged on.
- **Fixed-dose combination:** two drugs in one tablet.
- **Hazard ratio:** a risk ratio measured over time; below 1 means fewer events.
- **HbA1c:** blood test of average sugar over about three months.
- **Heart-failure guideline drug classes:** beta blocker, RAS blocker (ACE inhibitor or ARB) and MRA.
- **HWC:** health and wellness centre.
- **IHCI:** India Hypertension Control Initiative, a government programme with a fixed drug protocol.
- **INR:** clotting test that sets the warfarin dose.
- **Insulin inertia:** delay in starting or raising insulin.
- **Masked uncontrolled pressure:** high at home, normal in clinic.
- **NCD:** non-communicable disease.
- **Not significant:** small enough to be chance (a null result).
- **NT-proBNP:** a blood marker of heart strain.
- **Protocol:** a written step-by-step treatment plan.
- **Randomised trial:** people get treatments by chance.
- **Risk ratio:** risk with treatment divided by risk without; below 1 means lower risk.
- **SMART:** one inhaler for both maintenance and relief, so each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose.
- **Systolic:** the upper blood-pressure number, in mmHg (millimetres of mercury).
- **Time in range:** share of the day with sugar at 70-180 mg/dL.
- **Titration:** stepping a dose towards a target.

### A16. So what for us

OUR VIEW.
- **The fund asks for a routine treatment decision between visits,** from a home reading, by someone the patient can reach. Level 4 on the adaptive depth scale is the entry condition, however good the sensor (A2).
- **Blood pressure first.** On any count it is the largest pool: 35.5% of adults 20+, against 11.4% for diabetes on the same survey [D1-03-F01].
- **The leak is after treatment starts.** Two steps of the cascade leak, diagnosis and control. Over 95% of diagnosed Tamil Nadu patients are treated, yet the hypertension control rate was 35.4% (denominator not stated) [D1-03-F09]. The step from "treated" to "controlled" depends on the dose being raised and the medicine being taken, which is the decision our loop prepares.
- **Screening and enrolment are already huge** and run at crore scale [D1-03-F20]; the missing piece is the dose change between visits. A loop that feeds the existing protocol and records fits the system rather than competing with it.
- **The return visit is the bottleneck.** 51% of IHCI patients returned, and among those who returned control rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10]. Our loop must reach the half who do not come back, between visits. For blood pressure, the pilot should measure the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned.
- **The scarce thing is the prescriber's decision,** which waits for a visit that about half the patients do not make. About 80% of required rural CHC posts in four specialities (surgeon, physician, obstetrician-gynaecologist, paediatrician) were unfilled in March 2023 [D1-03-F16], and visits lasted about two minutes in 2013-2015 [D1-03-F24]. A two-minute visit has no time to read two weeks of home readings. Software should prepare the next protocol step for a general doctor or nurse to approve, with the specialist owning the protocol.
- **Patient costs.** Avoided trips save patients money, but without a rupee figure per visit we cannot yet claim a saving.
- **Not only an Indian product.** Treated but not controlled is the gap in Japan too.
- **Heart failure.** A clear dose gap with high death rates, but safe titration needs lab values, so heart failure is a later protocol for the same engine.
- **Assume most patients do not own a cuff.** Only 18.1% used one even among clinic attenders [D3-04-F06]. The loop must bring the cuff, the teaching and the thresholds.
- **Feeling well** recurs as a reason to stop, and a home reading is one thing that can contradict it.
- **A doctor's approval cannot be assumed.** A doctor may not trust the state protocol, so each proposal must show why the step is safe, answering the fears of slow control and side effects [D3-04-F15].
- **Never rely on a reminder alone.** WhatsApp reminders did not raise attendance [D3-04-F50]. A message only works if it reaches the person who holds the phone and leads to a decision.
- **Design for the household phone.** 57.4% of rural women own a phone [D1-03-F42], so about four in ten do not (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 57.4 = 42.6%). The design must work on a shared phone, through a health worker, and by voice, in the local language [D3-04-F05, D3-04-F23].
- **Risk: home readings bring bad news.** 21.8% of treated clinic attenders had masked uncontrolled pressure [D3-04-F09]; expect fear of more drugs and the urge to stop [D3-04-F02].

## Appendix B. The clinical evidence in detail

This appendix holds the detail behind chapter 2.1 (what actually improves outcomes) and chapter 2.2 (how care has been scaled without specialists). B1 to B10 cover what works, with every trial's design, size, place, comparator, length, confidence interval (CI) and limits, including the null results. B11 to B17 cover how care has been scaled without specialists, in India and abroad. B18 sets out what a doctor would ask. The burden figures and the Indian cohorts are in Appendix A.

### B1. The loop: sense, decide, confirm, act, learn

A therapy loop has five stages. This section says what happens at each and where existing products stop (picture in chapter 1: monitoring stops at the reading; a therapy loop changes the treatment).

- **Sense.** A home device gives a number, valid only if taken correctly. Level 1 products stop here (Appendix A2).
- **Decide.** Software applies a written protocol to this patient's readings and proposes the next step. Coaching apps decide advice, not doses [D1-04-F04]; the protocol model of the government's Simple app stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step ladder was found in it [D1-06-F40].
- **Confirm.** A doctor, nurse or health worker approves each change; unsafe cases go to a specialist. Trials used pharmacists [D1-01-F04] or village doctors [D1-01-F09]; no Indian service doing this from home readings was found [D1-04-F09].
- **Act.** The patient gets the new dose, medicine or exercise level. Heart-failure telemonitoring trials without a mandated dose protocol found no benefit (B6).
- **Learn.** The next readings show whether it worked, and the loop runs again. At 24 government-programme sites, 10,621 of 21,895 patients did not return [D1-03-F10].

### B2. Five rules the evidence gives

Across six disease areas, a home reading improved outcomes when it led to a changed treatment, and mostly did not when it was only displayed or turned into a reminder. OUR VIEW: five rules follow from that, each with its headline numbers. The full trials are in B4 to B9 and B14.

**1. The reading must change the treatment.** In 15 pooled trials, self-monitoring alone lowered systolic pressure 1.0 mmHg against usual care, no effect; self-monitoring with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or lifestyle counselling), not dose changes alone, lowered it 6.1 (B4) [D1-01-F05]. Two US heart-failure trials of remote monitoring without a mandated dose protocol found no benefit [D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33], while fast dose stepping after discharge cut readmission or death (B6) [D1-01-F27]. Against usual care, warfarin patients who set their own dose from home tests had fewer deaths; in separate trials, those who left the dose to the clinic did not; the two approaches were not compared head to head (B7) [D1-02-F05].

**2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics.** In a UK trial, sending readings electronically added a non-significant 1.2 mmHg over paper once the family doctor adjusted doses (B4) [D1-01-F03]. In rural China, supervised village doctors stepping drugs by protocol got 57.0% under 130/80, against 19.9% with enhanced usual care, and cardiovascular events were lower at 4 years, though the programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid incentives (B14) [D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38]. The Indian null result belongs here: mWellcare gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps at the visit, and found no benefit over enhanced usual care. What that null result does and does not show is in B14 [D1-01-F46].

**3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes.** Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care, and inhaler reminders raised children's adherence with no difference in school absence (B9) [D1-02-F59, D1-02-F01]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision ("is the current dose being taken before we raise it"), not a product.

**4. Someone must pay for the outcome.** Apps and sensors sold on their own failed. Pear's assets fetched just over $6 million against $130 million of liabilities (2023-2024; B8) [D1-02-F42]; Teva withdrew the Digihaler app and stopped US distribution of its sensor inhalers on 1 June 2024 [D1-02-F41]. Those at scale are paid by employers and insurers for clinician-led programmes (Hinge Health: revenue $234.970 million in the third quarter of 2026 [D1-05-F15, D1-05-F16]) or sell a therapy device (Insulet: $842.0 million [D1-05-F41]). The companies are in Appendix D and the payers in Appendix E.

**5. People stay when their own clinician is in it.** In 8 remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants) median retention was 5.5 days; clinician referral added 40 days, payment 22 days (one study) [D1-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape. More retention figures are in B9.

### B3. A map of feedback-driven therapies

Five kinds of feedback-driven therapy, sorted by what the loop changes.

| What changes | Home signal | How fast it responds | Proof | Who decides |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Drug dose or protocol step | Cuff, fasting sugar, INR (clotting test), weight | Days to weeks: insulin every 3 days in a 2025 US rule [D1-06-F16]; blood pressure re-checked at 30 days [D1-06-F14] | Strong: randomised trials with fewer deaths, clots or hospital stays [D1-01-F38, D1-01-F27, D1-02-F05] | Patient on an agreed plan, pharmacist, nurse or health worker [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F04, D1-02-F06, D1-01-F09] |
| 2. Food and behaviour | Glucose sensor, step count | Each meal [D1-01-F22] | Mixed: a company-linked Indian trial cut HbA1c 2.9 points against 0.3 with standard care (B5) [D1-01-F19]; a US review of type 2 tools without a continuous sensor was negative (B5) [D1-01-F40] | App, coach |
| 3. Exercise as the dose | Camera, pulse, effort rating | Each session [D1-06-F36] | Matches in-person care; no better than usual care (pooled stroke trials, B7) [D1-02-F07] | Therapist or app [D1-02-F54] |
| 4. Therapy delivered by the device (closed-loop insulin pump) | Glucose sensor | Automatic | Strong: against a sensor alone, a dose algorithm cut HbA1c a further 0.6 points (B5) [D1-01-F43] | Algorithm, within clinician-set limits [D1-05-F41] |
| 5. Biofeedback (a body signal shown back to the patient) | Breathing or pulse sensor | During practice [D1-02-F15] | Weak: guided breathing had no blood-pressure effect once maker-linked trials were excluded (B7) [D1-02-F11] | Patient |

OUR VIEW: proof is strongest in kinds 1 and 4, where a drug dose with a known effect is changed and the signal is cheap, valid and fast. Kind 4 needs expensive hardware; kind 1 needs almost none. A student team, and a low-resource country, should start there.

### B4. Blood pressure: home readings that change the medicine

Blood pressure has the deepest evidence: primary-care titration trials, a 33,995-person trial of dose stepping by village doctors with four-year hard outcomes, and South Asian and Indian trials, including a null result that shows where a product should not try to add value. This section covers trials where a home reading changed the medicine; dose stepping by non-specialists at scale, and the South Asian and Indian trials, are in B14.

(Two pictures in chapter 2 belong here: the extra fall in systolic pressure against usual care by what was done with the reading, and the share of patients under control with and without a programme that steps the dose. They set separate trials with different patients and end points side by side, so compare the groups, not single bars.)

#### Trials where home readings led to a medicine change

| Trial, year | Country, setting | Patients | What changed, and who decided | Comparator | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TASMINH2, 2010 | UK, 24 general practices | 527, BP above 140/90 despite treatment | Patient self-titrated by a pre-agreed plan, with telemonitoring | Usual care | Systolic 3.7 mmHg lower at 6 months; 5.4 lower at 12 months (95% CI 2.4 to 8.5) [D1-01-F01] |
| TASMIN-SR, 2014 | UK, 59 practices | 552 at high cardiovascular risk (stroke, heart disease, diabetes, kidney disease) | Patient self-titrated by an individual algorithm, home target 120/75 | Usual care | 12-month BP 128.2/73.8 against 137.8/76.3; systolic 9.2 mmHg lower (5.7 to 12.7) [D1-01-F02] |
| TASMINH4, 2018 | UK, 142 practices | 1,182 | GP titrated from home readings, sent on paper or by telemonitoring | Usual care using clinic readings | Clinic systolic -3.5 mmHg (paper) and -4.7 (telemonitoring) at 12 months [D1-01-F03] |
| HyperLink, 2013 | USA, 16 primary care clinics, cluster trial | 450, uncontrolled BP | Pharmacists adjusted drugs from telemonitored home readings for 12 months | Usual care | Controlled 57.2% against 30.0% (at both 6 and 12 months); systolic -10.7 mmHg at 6 months, -9.7 at 12, -6.6 at 18 (six months after the service stopped) [D1-01-F04] |

Limits: TASMINH2 analysed completers only (91%) [D1-01-F01]; TASMIN-SR had primary data from 81% (8.8 mmHg with imputation) [D1-01-F02].

**The pooled analysis.** An analysis of individual patient data from 15 trials (7,138 people, 12 months) compared self-monitoring with usual care [D1-01-F05]:
- Self-monitoring alone: clinic systolic -1.0 mmHg (95% CI -3.3 to 1.2), no effect [D1-01-F05].
- Self-monitoring with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or lifestyle counselling), not dose changes alone: -6.1 mmHg (95% CI -9.0 to -3.2) [D1-01-F05].
- Self-monitoring worked best in people on fewer drugs and with baseline systolic up to 170 [D1-01-F05].

#### What telemonitoring adds once someone is titrating

Little. In TASMINH4, telemonitoring against paper self-monitoring, with the GP titrating in both arms, gave -1.2 mmHg (95% CI -3.5 to 1.2), not significant [D1-01-F03]. The independent US review by PHTI (Peterson Health Technology Institute, October 2024) rated monitoring-only programmes "not clinically meaningful", and said monitoring "may support adoption for providers who consistently act on monitoring data" [D1-01-F39]. It rated medication-management programmes, where virtual care teams adjust drugs, "clinically meaningful and more rapid", against a threshold of a 5 mmHg systolic fall [D1-01-F39]. It also names Omron VitalSight as a monitoring product (level 1 in Appendix A2) [D1-01-F39].

#### A lifestyle-only prescription app in Japan

HERB-DH1 tested CureApp HT, an app giving personalised lifestyle coaching with no drug change (adaptive depth 3), in 390 untreated adults with hypertension at 12 sites in Japan, open-label, for 12 weeks [D1-01-F07]. Against lifestyle advice alone: 24-hour ambulatory systolic -2.4 mmHg (95% CI -4.5 to -0.3), home -4.3, office -3.6; no major programme-related safety events to 24 weeks [D1-01-F07]. CureApp HT was approved in April 2022 and covered by national health insurance from 1 September 2022, prescribed by doctors (THEIR CLAIM for "first worldwide") [D1-01-F57]. A price of about 8,000 yen, with the patient paying 30%, appears in a search summary only [D1-01-F57]; the company's June 2026 release gives 7,010 yen for the app as an insured material (THEIR CLAIM) [D2-04-F43].

OUR VIEW: it moved BP about half as much as the titration trials, in patients not yet on drugs; depth 3 helps a little but does not replace dose changes.

#### Home blood pressure in an Indian diabetes trial

A secondary analysis of a company-linked Indian diabetes trial (Twin Health) used home BP to guide drug changes: systolic -7.6 against -3.2 mmHg, in small subgroups [D1-01-F20].

### B5. Diabetes

In type 2 diabetes the same split holds: software that changes the insulin dose works, and monitoring or coaching alone gives small gains. Closed-loop insulin, where the device changes the dose itself every few minutes, is the model case of an adaptive therapy.

#### Insulin-dose software (adaptive depth 4)

- **d-Nav, 2019:** randomised trial, 181 adults on insulin with HbA1c 7.5-11%, 3 US centres, 6 months. A handheld device measured glucose and computed the next dose, plus clinician support, against clinician support alone (both arms 7 contacts). HbA1c fell 1.0% against 0.3% (p<0.0001); low blood sugar 0.29 against 0.29 events a month. Funded by the US NIH; the authors are maker-linked [D1-01-F13].
- **TeleDiab-2, 2019:** randomised, 191 adults starting basal (long-acting) insulin, 4 months. A phone voice system and an app both proposed daily dose changes towards a fasting glucose of about 100 mg/dL. HbA1c -1.44% and -1.48% against -0.92% with standard care. No severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F14]. The country (France) comes from the research agent's knowledge, not the abstract [D1-01-F14].
- **Sanofi My Dose Coach** has observational data only: in the US, 2,517 users, 44% reached their fasting target, low blood sugar in 12-16% of users [D1-01-F15]; in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, 494 users, 55.9% reached target in a mean 14.8 days, low blood sugar 1.4% [D1-01-F16]. Neither had a control group. Its status in India is unknown (search summary only) [D1-04-F09].

#### Glucose sensors with and without an algorithm

- **Sensor alone (CGM, continuous glucose monitor), not on insulin:** IMMEDIATE, 116 adults, 16 weeks, time in range up 9.9 points, HbA1c 0.3% lower (95% CI 0 to 0.7) [D1-01-F17].
- **Sensor alone, on basal insulin:** MOBILE, 175 adults, 15 US centres, 8 months: HbA1c 0.4% lower (-0.8 to -0.1). Funded by Dexcom, the sensor maker [D1-01-F42]. This is the one exception to "self-monitoring alone has no effect".
- **Sensor plus algorithm:** 2IQP, 2025, 319 adults with type 2 diabetes on insulin, US and Canada, 13 weeks. Automated insulin delivery against own insulin method, with a sensor in both arms. HbA1c 0.6 points lower (-0.8 to -0.4); time in range 14 points higher. Funded by Tandem, the pump maker [D1-01-F43]. Because both arms had a sensor, this isolates what the dose-changing algorithm adds.

#### Closed loop as the model case

In type 1 diabetes, Control-IQ (168 people, 6 months) raised time in range by 11 points against a sensor-augmented pump and ran in closed-loop mode 90% of the time [D1-01-F24]. The iLet bionic pancreas (326 people, 13 weeks) started from body weight alone with no carbohydrate counting and lowered HbA1c by 0.5 [D1-01-F25]. In type 2 diabetes, a 26-person crossover trial with no meal doses gave time in range 66.3% against 32.3% [D1-01-F26]. A 2026 review says the American Diabetes Association now supports automated delivery as the preferred method for some type 2 patients; the ADA text itself was not opened [D1-01-F45].

#### Nutrition and "digital twin" results, with caveats

- **Zeevi 2015, Israel, 800 people:** a model predicted each person's post-meal glucose; HbA1c was not the outcome [D1-01-F22]. **ZOE METHOD** (347 US adults, mostly without diabetes, company-sponsored): triglycerides -0.13 mmol/L [D1-01-F55].
- **Twin Health, India,** 319 people, open-label, 2:1: HbA1c -2.9 against -0.3 with standard care at 1 year, and "72.7% remission"; the remission definition and drug-withdrawal rules are not in the abstract, and author company links were not checked [D1-01-F19].
- **Twin Health, Cleveland Clinic,** 150 people, single site: HbA1c 6.5% or under on no drug except metformin, 71% against 2.4%. Read through a trade article only [D1-01-F56].
- **Virta:** not randomised (262 against 87, self-selected). At 2 years, use of diabetes drugs other than metformin fell from 55.7% to 26.8% [D1-01-F21].

#### The independent verdict

PHTI (March 2024) found US digital tools for type 2 diabetes without a continuous glucose monitor "do not deliver clinically meaningful benefits and result in a higher cost than usual care", with gains "minimal and short-term" [D1-01-F40]. The two exceptions were people with higher HbA1c newly starting insulin, and nutritional ketosis programmes [D1-01-F40]. PHTI's new review of sensor and GLP-1 support reports in 2027 [D1-01-F41].

### B6. Heart failure

Heart failure gives the sharpest contrast in the notes: fast dose stepping cut death or readmission by a third, while several large telemonitoring trials without a mandated dose protocol were null.

#### Fast dose stepping

STRONG-HF (2022) was an open-label trial in 87 hospitals in 14 countries with 1,078 patients admitted with acute heart failure [D1-01-F27]. The high-intensity arm raised drugs to full recommended doses within 2 weeks of discharge, with 4 visits in 2 months checking symptoms, lab tests and NT-proBNP (a blood marker of heart strain). At day 90, full doses: RAS blockers 55% against 2%, beta blockers 49% against 4%. Readmission or death at 180 days: 15.2% against 23.3% (adjusted estimates, not raw shares), RR 0.66 (0.50 to 0.86); the high-intensity arm also reported more side effects, 41% against 29% (B10). The trial stopped early for benefit. Funder: Roche Diagnostics, maker of NT-proBNP tests [D1-01-F27]. Benefit by age: HR 0.51 under 65, 0.73 over 65, no significant difference [D1-01-F28].

A Russian chatbot titration trial (66 patients, 6 weeks) saw 2 against 16 decompensations or deaths but lost 7 of 33 remote patients [D1-01-F51].

#### Telemonitoring: positive and negative trials

| Trial | Patients, place | What happened to the reading | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| TELE-HF, 2010 | 1,653, USA, 180 days | Daily symptoms and weight by phone, reviewed by patients' own clinicians | Readmission or death 52.3% against 51.5%, null [D1-01-F32] |
| BEAT-HF, 2016 | 1,437, California, 180 days | BP, pulse, weight reviewed by central nurses with protocol actions and phone calls; no mandated dose protocol | Readmission aHR 1.03, null; better quality of life [D1-01-F33] |
| GUIDE-HF, 2021 | 1,000, US and Canada | Implanted lung-artery pressure sensor guiding care | HR 0.88 (0.74 to 1.05), neutral overall [D1-01-F34] |
| TIM-HF2, 2018 | 1,571, Germany | Structured remote management | Days lost ratio 0.80 (p=0.046); all-cause death HR 0.70 (0.50 to 0.96) [D1-01-F30] |

OUR VIEW on what separates them: the positive trials had a structured team or explicit dose targets; the null ones sent data to clinicians or nurses without a mandated dose protocol (BEAT-HF's nurses did follow protocol actions). TIM-HF2's benefit grew with distance to a cardiologist, 13% lower risk per doubling of distance [D1-01-F31]. The TELE-HF authors stressed "a thorough, independent evaluation of disease-management strategies before their adoption" [D1-01-F32].

#### Pooled analyses, which conflict

A 2026 meta-analysis of 79 trials (31,669 patients) found remote monitoring cut heart-failure admissions (IRR 0.81) and death (RR 0.90) with no difference by method [D1-01-F53]. Another 2026 meta-analysis of 16 trials (8,618) found a gradient: pressure-guided RR 0.71, structured remote management 0.79, non-invasive telemonitoring alone 0.93, not significant; the authors wrote "passive telemonitoring alone is insufficient" [D1-01-F54]. They used different trial sets [D1-01-F54].

#### The Indian treatment gap

Indian registries show patients discharged on too few guideline drugs, with high death rates, and they report drug classes, not dose levels. The registry table is in Appendix A7 [D1-01-F35, D1-01-F47, D1-01-F48, D1-01-F49, D1-01-F50].

### B7. Other conditions

The other conditions repeat the pattern and add two lessons: a dose loop can work with no sensor at all, and rehabilitation by software matches in-person care without beating usual care.

- **Warfarin.** A Cochrane review of 28 trials (8,950 patients) found that patients who tested INR (a blood-clotting test) at home and adjusted their own dose by a schedule had fewer clots (RR 0.47) and lower death (RR 0.55, 8 trials). Patients who tested at home and left the dose to the clinic had fewer clots (RR 0.69) but no change in death (RR 0.94, 3 trials). Each approach was compared with usual care in separate sets of trials, not with each other. Major bleeding did not change overall (RR 0.95) [D1-02-F05].
- **Gout.** In a UK trial (517 patients, Nottingham, 2 years), nurses titrating urate-lowering drugs to a target reached it in 95% against 30% under GP care, RR 3.18, at £5,066 per quality-adjusted life year. It was not digital: it was a protocol run by nurses [D1-02-F06].
- **Asthma and COPD.** SMART (one inhaler for both maintenance and relief, so each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose) cut exacerbations by RR 0.68 in 16 trials with 22,748 people aged 12 and over [D1-02-F37]. No sensor was needed because the patient's own reliever use is the signal and the inhaler delivers the dose change at that moment. Sensor inhalers did less: reminders raised adherence without changing school absence (B9) [D1-02-F01]; the Digihaler system's odds ratio for control was 1.35, with a credible interval of 0.846 to 2.038 crossing 1, and adherence fell from 79.2% to 68.6% over 6 months [D1-02-F02]; a Propeller trial cut reliever use but not asthma control scores overall (company-affiliated authors) [D1-02-F38]. Commercially, Teva's sensor inhalers were withdrawn (B2, rule 4) [D1-02-F41], and an undated ResMed page says Propeller "has ceased operations" [D1-02-F40].
- **Rehabilitation by software.** Stroke telerehab after discharge (pooled trials, 661 people) was no better than usual care for daily-living activities (SMD 0.00) and about equal to in-person physiotherapy [D1-02-F07]. Lung telerehab, 99% COPD, matched centre rehab on walking distance, with completion 93% against 70% [D1-02-F03]. A Sword Health trial (140 back-pain patients, company-affiliated) found no difference in disability against in-person physiotherapy but lower dropout, 15.7% against 34.3% [D1-02-F08]. PHTI (June 2024) found physiotherapist-guided virtual care comparable to in-person care with lower spending, app-only exercise "unlikely to be effective as total substitutes", and did not separate the effect of adapting exercise to measured performance [D1-02-F54].
- **Biofeedback and stimulation.** Device-guided breathing lowered systolic BP by 3.67 mmHg across 8 trials (494 people), but showed no effect once the 5 manufacturer-linked trials were removed [D1-02-F11]. Nerivio, a sham-controlled migraine stimulator, gave pain relief at 2 hours in 66.7% against 38.8%, but it uses no sensor loop [D1-02-F12].

### B8. Prescription apps

Software sold as a prescribed treatment has passed trials, yet most of the companies behind it failed. The table lists the products in the notes; "status" is the regulatory status where the notes give it.

| Product (company) | Treats | Status in notes | Pivotal effect | What happened to the company |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| reSET, Somryst (Pear, US) | Addiction; insomnia | Not stated | reSET abstinence OR 1.62 [D1-02-F17]; Somryst 56.6% insomnia remission at 1 year [D1-02-F18] | Chapter 11 in April 2023; assets sold for "just over $6 million" against $130M liabilities [D1-02-F42] |
| EndeavorRx (Akili, US) | ADHD in children | De Novo 2020 | Attention test score up 0.88, a computerised test rather than parent or teacher ratings [D1-02-F45] | 2023 prescription revenue $523,000; sale for about $34M announced May 2024, completed 2 July 2024 [D1-02-F44] |
| AspyreRx (Better Therapeutics, US) | Type 2 diabetes | Cleared 2023 | HbA1c 0.39 points better than a control app at 90 days [D1-02-F21] | Expected no revenue in 2023 (revenue not reported); wind-down considered, March 2024, then wound down [D1-02-F46]; assets to Click, terms undisclosed [D1-02-F47] |
| SleepioRx, DaylightRx (Big Health) | Insomnia; anxiety | Says it is among 9 FDA-cleared products (THEIR CLAIM) | Sleep efficiency +20% against +6% [D1-02-F19]; anxiety d=1.08 against a waitlist [D1-02-F20] | Medicare codes from 1 January 2025; $23.7M raised February 2026 (search summary only) [D1-02-F52] |
| Rejoyn (Otsuka, Click) | Depression, add-on | FDA clearance April 2024 [D1-02-F48] | Primary result p=0.0568, not significant; supportive analysis p=0.0211 (from a secondary copy of the FDA summary) [D1-02-F49] | Sales NOT FOUND |
| Motivista (Click) | Negative symptoms of schizophrenia | FDA clearance, announced October 2026 | 457 patients, 6.8 against 4.2 points, d -0.36 [D1-02-F50] | Too new |
| CureApp Smoking (Japan) | Smoking | Not stated | Abstinence 63.9% against 50.5%, OR 1.73; uses an exhaled carbon monoxide checker [D1-02-F22] | NOT SEARCHED [D1-02-F53] |
| CureApp HT (Japan) | Hypertension | Approved April 2022, insured September 2022 (B4) [D1-01-F57] | Ambulatory systolic -2.4 mmHg (B4) [D1-02-F23] | NOT SEARCHED [D1-02-F53] |

The research note records that none of these changes a drug dose (D1-02, note under its trial table). Most deliver scripted therapy content at adaptive depth 2-3.

### B9. Drop-off and adherence technology

People stop using health apps quickly, and the trials show that raising adherence on its own often leaves outcomes unchanged.

#### Retention

- 93 Android mental-health apps with 10,000 or more installs (2019): the median app kept 3.3% of users at day 30 [D1-02-F26].
- Eight remote US studies: median retention 5.5 days, with clinician referral adding 40 days (B2, rule 5) [D1-02-F27].
- Chronic-disease app trials: pooled dropout 43% (40% in randomised trials, 49% in observational studies) [D1-02-F28].
- Engagement strategies helped modestly, SMD 0.33, very low certainty [D1-02-F56].
- With a clinician in the loop, retention was higher: Sword dropout 15.7% [D1-02-F08]; lung telerehab completion 93% [D1-02-F03] (both in B7).

#### Adherence rose; outcomes did not

| Trial | Patients | Adherence result | Outcome result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inhaler reminders, New Zealand, 2015 | 220 children, 6 months | 84% against 30% | School absence 1.9% against 1.7% of days, no difference [D1-02-F01] |
| MedISAFE-BP reminder app, US, 2018 | 411 adults, 12 weeks, against control | Adherence score +0.4 | Systolic -0.5 mmHg, p=0.78, not significant [D1-01-F06] |
| TB pillbox, China, 2015 | 4,173, 36 districts | Missed doses 17.0% against 29.9% (aMR 0.58); text messages no effect | Cure not measured. The planned step (doctor moves non-adherent patients to intensive management) was "underutilised" [D1-02-F34] |
| ASCENT TB, four countries, 2025 | 23,483 | Smart pillboxes or medication labels, against standard of care | Poor outcomes not reduced (adjusted ratios 1.13 to 1.49, all intervals crossing 1); two social harms from pillbox disclosure [D1-02-F59] |
| 99DOTS phone-based adherence, 2025 | Interrupted time series, not randomised | 87.2% enrolled | Completion 89.8% against 87.1% before; no change in treatment success [D1-02-F58] |

No trial in the notes changed a tuberculosis treatment from adherence data; in China the planned step was "underutilised" [D1-02-F34].

### B10. Safety

Every adverse-event finding from the titration and closed-loop trials in the notes.

| Area | Trial | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Blood pressure | TASMINH2 | Leg swelling 32% against 22% (p=0.022); other side effects similar [D1-01-F01] |
| Blood pressure | TASMIN-SR | "without excessive adverse events" [D1-01-F02] |
| Blood pressure | TASMINH4 | Adverse events similar in all arms [D1-01-F03] |
| Blood pressure | CRHCP, 18 months | No treatment-related serious adverse events [D1-01-F09] |
| Blood pressure | CRHCP, 4 years | No difference in injurious falls, symptomatic low BP, fainting or kidney outcomes [D1-01-F38] |
| Insulin | d-Nav | Low blood sugar 0.29 against 0.29 events a month [D1-01-F13] |
| Insulin | TeleDiab-2 | No severe low blood sugar; mild episodes similar [D1-01-F14] |
| Insulin | My Dose Coach, no control | Low blood sugar in 12-16% of US users [D1-01-F15], 1.4% in the Gulf [D1-01-F16] |
| Closed loop | Control-IQ; iLet | Time below 70 mg/dL fell; 1 diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA, a dangerous acid build-up) [D1-01-F24]. Severe low blood sugar 17.7 against 10.8 per 100 patient-years, not significant [D1-01-F25] |
| Closed loop, type 2 | CamAPS HX; 2IQP; twiist | 1 serious adverse event [D1-01-F26]; 1 severe low blood sugar [D1-01-F43]; 1 DKA, no control arm [D1-01-F44] |
| Heart failure | STRONG-HF | Any adverse event by day 90: 41% against 29%; serious 16% against 17%; fatal 5% against 6% [D1-01-F27]; similar by age [D1-01-F28] |
| Heart failure | Chatbot titration, Russia | Potassium and kidney function no different at 6 weeks [D1-01-F51] |

Potassium and kidney event rates by arm in STRONG-HF are not in the notes (B19).
